Preregistered Belief Revision Contracts

Saad Alqithami Email: alqithami@gmail.com
Abstract

Multi-agent language-model systems can change their answers in response to social cues without acquiring new externally validated evidence. We study PBRC (Preregistered Belief Revision Contracts), which associate public evidence conditions with permitted updates to an explicit belief state. A router enforces the selected contract branch and records a certificate for each accepted non-fallback transition. Under evidence gating and an argmax-preserving fallback, token-empty interaction preserves the top-hypothesis set; a nonamplifying fallback also prevents growth of the specified confidence functional. We characterize these social-only properties by local transition conditions and distinguish behavior-preserving normal forms from safety-enforcing restrictions. For token-invariant contracts, identical validated-token exposure traces induce identical enforced trajectories under the specified routing assumptions. Under synchronous flooding, accumulated token knowledge follows ordinary distance reachability, whereas incoming exposure follows positive-length walks; this distinction yields exact trace characterizations and the standard tight diameter bound for universal knowledge closure. We give source-labelled accountability conditions for finite execution logs, prove soundness of a companion KD45/PDL specification system, and establish bounded assignment certificates for a guarded conjunctive trigger fragment. Controlled simulations and a matched synthetic study illustrate the conditional guarantees and vulnerability to correlated label errors. KAIROS experiments demonstrate token-empty answer retention on 3,000 rows. A separate 200-claim SciFact study records evidence-enabled admission: PBRC achieves 53.0% accuracy, versus 49.0% for RAW and 61.5% for clean RAG; its gain over RAW is statistically inconclusive, with 12 harmful and 20 beneficial answer changes. The framework governs external protocol state and accepted outputs; it does not by itself establish semantic truth, calibrated probabilities, or improved task accuracy.

   

Keywords belief revision ⋅\cdot dynamic doxastic logic ⋅\cdot protocol semantics ⋅\cdot auditability ⋅\cdot graph reachability ⋅\cdot multi-agent deliberation ⋅\cdot large language models.

1 Introduction

Deliberation can improve the information available to an agent, but it can also make agreement, confidence, prestige, or majority size substitutes for independently checkable reasons. Recent LLM studies report conformity and peer-pressure effects [Weng et al.(2025), Song et al.(2025)], including sensitivity to topology and self–social weighting [Han et al.(2026)]. Emergent conventions and collective biases are related but distinct phenomena [Ashery et al.(2025)]. These results motivate a protocol question: which changes to a public belief state should a deliberation system permit, and what evidence should accompany them?

We introduce PBRC, a public contract associating first-order event predicates with permitted update operators, a deterministic priority order, and a fallback. A triggered update requires a nonempty validated witness, full-event satisfaction of the selected trigger, and faithful execution of its operator. Fallback remains an explicit transition and may reduce confidence without changing the top set. Thus the framework controls the admissibility of externally represented transitions rather than asserting that every numerical change must carry new evidence.

The separation between communication and admissible revision is conditional. An evidential trigger merely requires the presence of a validated token; it can still depend on message metadata unless token invariance is imposed. A signature authenticates an artifact, but does not make its semantic label correct. A state-holding router enforces the public state, but does not directly constrain an LLM’s private reasoning. These distinctions delimit all claims below.

1.1 Contributions

We develop five connected results.

  1. 1.

    Contracts, witnesses, and enforcement. Section 4 separates full-event trigger selection, restricted witness checking, and numerical operator compliance. The default semantics uses an authoritative state-holding router.

  2. 2.

    Conditional social-only guarantees. Sections 6–7 prove top-set stability and maximum-confidence nonamplification under conservative fallback, and characterize these properties by the actually selected one-step transition (Theorem 6). Evidence gating is a sufficient design discipline, not a necessary syntactic form for every robust protocol.

  3. 3.

    Normal forms and licensed transitions. Section 8 gives behavior-preserving and enforcement-based translations under explicit witness and routing hypotheses. The former may absorb unsafe behavior into fallback; it does not create safety. Under faithful enforcement, each top-set change has an accepted certificate licensing that transition (Theorem 17).

  4. 4.

    Token-trace factorization and flooding. Token-invariant contracts separate rhetorical presentation from transition inputs under token-determined or complete routing. Incoming exposure is characterized by positive-length walk relations (Theorems 12 and 15); accumulated knowledge has the standard tight diameter bound (Corollary 6). Universal trace equivalence includes adjacency equality and is not claimed as a nontrivial graph compression.

  5. 5.

    Threat assumptions, specification, and checking. Sections 9–12 separate provenance, semantic correctness, replay age, and validator compromise. A KD45/PDL specification system is sound, and its belief-free fragment is checkable on faithful finite logs. Guarded existential triggers admit small assignment certificates with linear logical verification cost after lookup indexing; search and validation costs remain separate. Section 13 evaluates protocol behavior through controlled simulations, a matched synthetic study, and KAIROS and SciFact experiments.

Scope. The guarantees concern fixed finite hypothesis sets, public transition inputs, conservative fallback, and faithful enforcement. Truth preservation, statistical calibration, secure evidence generation, dynamic hypothesis expansion, and empirical benefit under new evidence require additional assumptions or evaluation. The logical results establish soundness and finite-model monitoring.

1.2 Relation to underlying revision operators

PBRC leaves the choice of numerical update operator to the contract designer. It is compatible with evidence aggregation but does not establish AGM rationality postulates for probability vectors, select a universally optimal inference rule, or make social consensus intrinsically evidential. It constrains a recorded transition according to public rules. The relation to runtime enforcement, evidence logics, and agent protocols is discussed next.

The operational model and contract semantics appear in Sections 3–4, followed by a worked example and the formal guarantees. Sections 9–12 address threats, monitoring, implementation, and cost. Section 13 presents the experimental methods and results. Appendix A gives the proofs of logical soundness and finite-model monitoring.

2 Related work

Empirical studies of LLM multi-agent systems (MAS) document systematic conformity and peer-pressure effects whose strength depends on the interaction protocol, peer reliability, rapport, and network structure. BenchForm provides a benchmarked characterization of conformity across interaction protocols [Weng et al.(2025)]. KAIROS studies peer-pressure under heterogeneous peer reliability and rapport [Song et al.(2025)]. Recent results also emphasize that topology and self–social weighting can modulate conformity and “wrong-but-sure” cascades [Han et al.(2026)]. Complementary work adapts classic social-psychology paradigms and reports that AI agents exhibit conformity patterns aligned with Social Impact Theory [Bellina et al.(2026)], connecting to foundational human-group evidence on conformity and social impact [Asch(1951), Latané(1981)]. Our contribution concerns admissibility rather than measuring conformity: PBRC specifies when a public state transition is licensed. Rhetoric independence additionally requires token-invariant predicates and operators.

Repeated interaction among LLM agents can also yield emergent conventions and collective biases [Ashery et al.(2025)]; the earlier preprint is a version of the same study [Ashery et al.(2024)]. These phenomena motivate mechanisms that distinguish coordination signals from epistemic justification. PBRC targets the epistemic side: contracts restrict which belief transitions are admissible and require certificates with validated evidence tokens, so convention formation cannot by itself justify epistemic flips absent evidence.

Belief revision and belief-change formalisms provide the canonical language for rational change of epistemic states. AGM belief revision axiomatizes rational postulates for theory change [Alchourrón et al.(1985), Gärdenfors(1988), Hansson(2026)]. Belief update distinguishes revising by new information from updating after world change [Katsuno and Mendelzon(1991)], and iterated revision studies sequential change [Darwiche and Pearl(1997)]. Ranking-theoretic approaches provide alternative representations of epistemic states and revision dynamics [Spohn(2012)]. Dynamic epistemic logic (DEL) models informational actions and announcements [Baltag and Renne(2026), van Ditmarsch et al.(2007)], and dynamic logics of belief change connect AGM-style ideas with dynamic and plausibility semantics in both single- and multi-agent settings [van Benthem and Smets(2015)]. PBRC does not propose a new underlying revision operator; instead it constrains which transitions are admissible under social interaction via preregistered, token-witnessable triggers, and it supports auditing via checkable certificates. Relatedly, belief merging and judgment aggregation study how to combine information from multiple sources under inconsistency [Konieczny and Pérez(2002), Konieczny and Pérez(2011)]; PBRC is compatible with such operators but adds an enforceable evidence gate for when they may be applied.

Runtime enforcement already studies monitors that restrict or transform executions according to specified policies [Schneider(2000), Ligatti et al.(2005)]. PBRC uses that established architecture for evidence-labelled transitions of a public belief state; the presence of a trusted gate is not itself a new enforcement theorem. Evidence-based dynamic logics also distinguish evidence structures from resulting beliefs [van Benthem and Pacuit(2011)]. Our contribution lies in the explicit combination of contract selection, validated token witnesses, router-held numerical state, and exposure-trace analysis, under the assumptions stated in each result.

Combining belief modalities with dynamic/program operators has a substantial history in dynamic doxastic logic and related systems [Leitgeb and Segerberg(2007), Schmidt and Tishkovsky(2008)]; see [Fagin et al.(1995), van Benthem(2011)] for broader background on multi-agent epistemic/doxastic logic and logical dynamics. Our novelty is not the presence of KD45 + PDL per se, but the use of program structure to encode PBRC contracts and to specify invariants over enforced, certificate-carrying belief transitions (Section 10).

Compliance monitoring in MAS is often framed in terms of commitment-based protocols and social/interactional commitments [Singh(1999), Yolum and Singh(2002)]. PBRC enables compliance monitoring for epistemic transitions: accepted non-fallback transitions require verifiable evidence tokens and witness sets that an external router or auditor can check; fallback can still change numerical confidence. This certificate discipline is reminiscent of proof-carrying mechanisms, where untrusted producers attach checkable artifacts enabling efficient validation by a consumer [Necula(1997)]. Tamper-evident audit logs are a standard accountability primitive [Schneier and Kelsey(1999)]; PBRC certificates are designed to be stored in such append-only logs. If one additionally wants to bind correct execution of updates (not just admissibility), verifiable computation and succinct proof systems provide relevant primitives [Gennaro et al.(2010), Parno et al.(2013)] (Section 4.4).

Trust and reputation models are another common response to unreliable peers in MAS [Sabater and Sierra(2005)]. PBRC takes a complementary stance: rather than granting epistemic force to socially mediated reputation, it treats reliability as an evidence problem to be expressed through verifiable artifacts (tool provenance, signed attestations, audited verifier judgments). Socially persuasive claims remain non-binding absent checkable evidence.

Our notion of “wrong-but-sure” cascades connects to classic informational cascades and herding in economics and social learning, where agents update based on others’ actions and can converge on incorrect beliefs [Banerjee(1992), Bikhchandani et al.(1992)]. Networked aggregation and Bayesian social learning further show how topology shapes convergence and error propagation [DeGroot(1974), Bala and Goyal(1998), Golub and Jackson(2010), Acemoglu et al.(2011)]. PBRC differs in that it does not prescribe a specific update rule; instead, it constrains which belief transitions are admissible via preregistered, checkable evidence triggers, yielding a factorization through token dissemination when the contract and router satisfy token invariance.

Recent LLM MAS often use debate/critique/reflection patterns to improve reasoning [Liang et al.(2023), Li et al.(2023), Shinn et al.(2023), Madaan et al.(2023)]. Practical orchestration frameworks operationalize such protocols in agentic programming settings [Wu et al.(2023), Hong et al.(2023)]. These approaches are typically implemented as prompting patterns without externally checkable admissibility constraints; PBRC is complementary, providing enforceable constraints that can prevent purely social persuasion steps absent admissible evidence.

Evidence tokens can be instantiated using retrieval-augmented and tool-augmented LLM pipelines, where snippets, citations, and tool outputs provide structured artifacts that a verifier can validate [Lewis et al.(2020), Yao et al.(2022), Nakano et al.(2021), Menick et al.(2022), Schick et al.(2023)]. Retrieval-and-revise methods and hallucination detectors can further serve as candidate verifiers or token labelers [Asai et al.(2024), Manakul et al.(2023)]. On the systems side, provenance standards such as W3C PROV provide a natural representation for evidence lineage [W3C(2013)]. PBRC abstracts these implementation details into a token interface (Valid\mathrm{Valid}/Supports\mathrm{Supports}/Contradicts\mathrm{Contradicts}/Type\mathrm{Type}/Fresh\mathrm{Fresh}) and studies protocol-level guarantees when admissibility is enforced via checkable certificates.

Taken together, these lines of work show that social interaction can induce conformity, cascades, and convention formation, while belief-change logics and systems mechanisms provide tools for specifying and enforcing rational updates. PBRC connects these perspectives by making social robustness and auditability enforceable at the protocol level: preregistered contracts specify which evidence patterns license which updates; routers enforce admissibility by routing token-empty steps to fallback; and auditors can inspect the accepted license alongside full transition inputs and outcomes.

3 Operational model: evidence-annotated deliberation

We formalize a deliberation run among agents who exchange messages containing evidence tokens. Tokens represent checkable artifacts (tool outputs, verified citations, signed sensor readings, etc.). The model separates persuasive language (unvalidated message content) from validated evidence (tokens that satisfy Valid\mathrm{Valid} under a router-side validity layer).

3.1 Agents, hypotheses, and beliefs

Let 𝒜={1,…,n}\mathcal{A}=\{1,\dots,n\} be agents and ℋ={h1,…,hm}\mathcal{H}=\{h_{1},\dots,h_{m}\} a finite hypothesis set. Each agent ii has a belief distribution bit∈Δ⁡(ℋ)b_{i}^{t}\in\Delta(\mathcal{H}) at round tt:

bit​(h)≥0,∑h∈ℋbit​(h)=1.b_{i}^{t}(h)\geq 0,\quad\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}}b_{i}^{t}(h)=1.

Define:

conf⁡(b):=maxh∈ℋ⁡b⁡(h),argmax⁡(b):={h∈ℋ:b⁡(h)=conf⁡(b)}.\mathrm{conf}(b):=\max_{h\in\mathcal{H}}b(h),\qquad\mathrm{argmax}(b):=\{h\in\mathcal{H}:b(h)=\mathrm{conf}(b)\}.

For distances between beliefs we use total variation:

TV⁡(b,b′):=12​∑h∈ℋ|b⁡(h)−b′​(h)|.\mathrm{TV}(b,b^{\prime}):=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}}|b(h)-b^{\prime}(h)|.

3.2 Belief state as a router-side artifact (LLM instantiation)

The formal object bit∈Δ⁡(ℋ)b_{i}^{t}\in\Delta(\mathcal{H}) is a protocol state used for deliberation, enforcement, and auditing. In deployed LLM-agent systems it is often unreasonable to assume that agents maintain stable, calibrated internal Bayesian beliefs, or that self-reported probabilities are trustworthy. PBRC does not require these assumptions: a router/orchestrator can maintain an authoritative belief state and compute contract updates itself (Section 4.4), while agents contribute candidate hypotheses, arguments, and evidence tokens.

Finite candidate sets.

When the task exposes a finite set of candidates (multiple choice, ranked options, tool-selected actions), let ℋ\mathcal{H} be the candidate set and let the router maintain a score vector sit​(h)∈ℝs_{i}^{t}(h)\in\mathbb{R} (e.g., log-probabilities from the LLM, an auxiliary verifier model, or a task-specific scoring function). Define bit=softmax⁡(sit)b_{i}^{t}=\mathrm{softmax}(s_{i}^{t}) (optionally after calibration). In this setting, the belief distribution is fully external and auditable.

Open-ended tasks and dynamic hypothesis sets.

For open-ended tasks, a practical pattern is to maintain a dynamic hypothesis set ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t} produced by candidate generation and pruning. A proposed extension would treat hypothesis introduction as a contract-governed operation: new hypotheses may enter ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t} only when an evidential trigger fires (e.g., a validated retrieval token that introduces a new entity/answer), while social-only rounds cannot expand ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t}. Formally, one can model each episode as a sequence of stages, each with a fixed finite hypothesis set. A stage-transition operator (triggered by evidence) expands ℋ\mathcal{H} and reinitializes bb over the expanded set. The theorems below apply within each fixed stage. Correctness of an expansion or reinitialization operator requires a separate specification and is not established here.

Takeaway.

The fixed finite ℋ\mathcal{H} in the core theorems should be read as a stage-wise view: candidates are explicitly managed by the router and expanded only under evidential triggers.

3.3 Evidence tokens and first-order annotations

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a universe of evidence tokens and ℳ\mathcal{M} a universe of messages. We use a many-sorted first-order signature with sorts:

𝖠𝗀,𝖳𝗈𝗄,𝖬𝗌𝗀,𝖧𝗒𝗉,𝖳𝗂𝗆𝖾,𝖲𝖼𝗁𝖾𝗆𝖺,𝖢𝗈𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗑𝗍.\mathsf{Ag},\;\mathsf{Tok},\;\mathsf{Msg},\;\mathsf{Hyp},\;\mathsf{Time},\;\mathsf{Schema},\;\mathsf{Context}.

Predicates include:

Send⁡(a,b,m,t)\displaystyle\mathrm{Send}(a,b,m,t) agent a sends message m to b at time t,\displaystyle\text{agent $a$ sends message $m$ to $b$ at time $t$},
HasTok⁡(m,τ)\displaystyle\mathrm{HasTok}(m,\tau) m contains token τ,\displaystyle\text{$m$ contains token $\tau$},
Valid⁡(τ)\displaystyle\mathrm{Valid}(\tau) τ is externally verifiable under the validity layer,\displaystyle\text{$\tau$ is externally verifiable under the validity layer},
Supports⁡(τ,h),Contradicts⁡(τ,h)\displaystyle\mathrm{Supports}(\tau,h),\ \mathrm{Contradicts}(\tau,h) τ supports/contradicts hypothesis h,\displaystyle\text{$\tau$ supports/contradicts hypothesis $h$},
Type⁡(τ,κ)\displaystyle\mathrm{Type}(\tau,\kappa) τ has schema/type κ (e.g., tool vs. retrieval).\displaystyle\text{$\tau$ has schema/type $\kappa$ (e.g., tool vs.\ retrieval)}.
Events and token projection.

At each round tt, agent ii receives a multiset Eit⊆ℳE_{i}^{t}\subseteq\mathcal{M} (its event). Define the set of tokens mentioned in an event and the subset that validate:

𝒯all​(E):={τ∈𝒯:∃m∈E​HasTok​(m,τ)},𝒯⁡(E):={τ∈𝒯all​(E):Valid⁡(τ)}.\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{all}}(E)\;:=\;\{\,\tau\in\mathcal{T}:\exists m\in E\ \mathrm{HasTok}(m,\tau)\,\},\qquad\mathcal{T}(E)\;:=\;\{\,\tau\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{all}}(E):\mathrm{Valid}(\tau)\,\}.

The validated tokens available to agent ii at time tt are 𝒯it:=𝒯⁡(Eit)\mathcal{T}_{i}^{t}:=\mathcal{T}(E_{i}^{t}).

Events as finite relational structures.

To interpret first-order triggers, associate to each event EitE_{i}^{t} a finite relational structure 𝒮⁡(Eit)\mathcal{S}(E_{i}^{t}) whose domains are: agents 𝒜\mathcal{A}, message occurrences in EitE_{i}^{t}, tokens in 𝒯all​(Eit)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{all}}(E_{i}^{t}), hypotheses ℋ\mathcal{H}, the current and token-issue times used in the event, the finite public schema vocabulary, and the fixed public context identifiers. Predicates such as Send\mathrm{Send} and HasTok\mathrm{HasTok} are interpreted from message metadata, while Valid\mathrm{Valid}, Supports\mathrm{Supports}, and Contradicts\mathrm{Contradicts} are interpreted via the external validity/labeling layer. We write

Eit⊧φiff𝒮⁡(Eit)⊧φE_{i}^{t}\models\varphi\quad\text{iff}\quad\mathcal{S}(E_{i}^{t})\models\varphi

under Tarskian semantics with explicitly permitted empty message and token sorts: existential quantification over an empty sort is false and universal quantification is true. Each message occurrence has its own identifier, so multiplicity is represented even when message text repeats. Triggers use no token-sort constants or token-valued functions; token identities can be tested through relational attributes. This makes restriction to a witness subset well-defined. All non-token constants belong to their fixed public domains.

The event also fixes the instance identifier, current time, validator version, and semantic annotations used by the router. Comparisons of events in invariance results hold this public context fixed (or compare matching context at each round). Token identity alone does not justify equating different label interpretations or fresh and expired uses. The static flooding results additionally assume fixed validity and annotations during their horizon.

3.3.1 Concrete instantiation: typed tokens and entailment-based labeling

The abstract interface above—a validity predicate Valid⁡(τ)\mathrm{Valid}(\tau) together with Supports/Contradicts\mathrm{Supports}/\mathrm{Contradicts}—allows different evidence representations. The following design uses typed records and entailment-based labels for LLM-mediated tasks. Section 13.10 evaluates a restricted answer-level instantiation with retrieved passages and NLI labels; authenticated provenance remains an additional requirement for adversarial deployments. The formal results use the abstract interface and their explicit soundness assumptions.

Token typing.

Treat evidence tokens as typed, self-describing records with explicit provenance, e.g.:

  • •

    ToolResult⁡(tool,input_hash,output,output_hash,ts,sig)\mathrm{ToolResult}(\textsf{tool},\textsf{input\_hash},\textsf{output},\textsf{output\_hash},\textsf{ts},\textsf{sig}): a deterministic tool invocation with authenticated I/O.

  • •

    RetrievedSnippet⁡(source_id,url_hash,snippet,snippet_hash,ts,sig)\mathrm{RetrievedSnippet}(\textsf{source\_id},\textsf{url\_hash},\textsf{snippet},\textsf{snippet\_hash},\textsf{ts},\textsf{sig}): a retrieval return from an allowed source with immutable snippet hashing.

  • •

    VerifierJudgment⁡(verifier_id,claim,context_hash,label,conf,model_hash,sig)\mathrm{VerifierJudgment}(\textsf{verifier\_id},\textsf{claim},\textsf{context\_hash},\textsf{label},\textsf{conf},\textsf{model\_hash},\textsf{sig}): an authenticated judgment (e.g., NLI entailment) binding the label to a specific claim and context.

The contract fixes admissible token schemas and the authentication mechanism for each schema.

Validity.

Valid⁡(τ)\mathrm{Valid}(\tau) checks (i) schema well-formedness, (ii) authenticity of sig, and (iii) type-specific replay/consistency conditions. Examples: for ToolResult\mathrm{ToolResult}, (iii) may include deterministic re-execution or recomputation to confirm output_hash; for RetrievedSnippet\mathrm{RetrievedSnippet}, (iii) binds the snippet to an allowed source and time window; for VerifierJudgment\mathrm{VerifierJudgment}, (iii) binds the judgment to a pinned model_hash and an exact context_hash.

Supports/Contradicts via a deterministic labeling pipeline.

For tool tokens, Supports/Contradicts\mathrm{Supports}/\mathrm{Contradicts} is a deterministic mapping from structured tool outputs to hypotheses. For retrieval tokens, a simple auditable pattern is: (i) canonicalize hh into a natural-language claim 𝖼𝗅𝖺𝗂𝗆⁡(h)\mathsf{claim}(h); (ii) run a pinned NLI model on (premise=snippet, hypothesis=𝖼𝗅𝖺𝗂𝗆⁡(h)\mathsf{claim}(h)); (iii) threshold entailment/contradiction scores to produce label∈{entails,contradicts,neutral}\textsf{label}\in\{\textsf{entails},\textsf{contradicts},\textsf{neutral}\}; and (iv) emit a signed VerifierJudgment\mathrm{VerifierJudgment} token. Then define

Supports⁡(τ,h)​iff​τ​ is a VerifierJudgment with label entails and conf ≥θsup,\mathrm{Supports}(\tau,h)\ \text{iff}\ \tau\text{ is a VerifierJudgment with label entails and conf }\geq\theta_{\mathrm{sup}},

and analogously for Contradicts⁡(τ,h)\mathrm{Contradicts}(\tau,h) at threshold θcon\theta_{\mathrm{con}}.

Partial/uncertain evidence and “semantic laundering.”

Binary predicates can be coarse. This instantiation retains the verifier confidence conf and supports multi-attestation or kk-of-KK checks (Section 9) for high-impact updates (e.g., belief flips), making agreement and provenance inspectable. Agreement among correlated or fallible semantic verifiers is not a proved truth guarantee; the compromise bounds below apply only under their stated independence and honest-validator assumptions.

Minimal token interface.

A compact schema sufficient for many deployments is

τ=⟨type,payload,provenance,time,sig⟩,\tau=\langle\mathrm{type},\mathrm{payload},\mathrm{provenance},\mathrm{time},\mathrm{sig}\rangle,

where sig\mathrm{sig} is a validator signature or checkable attestation. The validity layer computes Valid⁡(τ)\mathrm{Valid}(\tau) router-side. The relations Supports⁡(τ,h)\mathrm{Supports}(\tau,h) and Contradicts⁡(τ,h)\mathrm{Contradicts}(\tau,h) can be computed deterministically from a typed payload, or can themselves be asserted by a signed label (as in VerifierJudgment\mathrm{VerifierJudgment}).

Semantic mismatch is an explicit failure mode.

Even if Valid⁡(τ)\mathrm{Valid}(\tau) holds, the semantic interpretation of τ\tau (and hence Supports/Contradicts\mathrm{Supports}/\mathrm{Contradicts}) can be wrong or irrelevant. PBRC does not eliminate semantic alignment risk; it localizes it to the validity/labeling layer and makes it auditable (Section 9).

3.4 Token-empty events (social-only)

Definition 1 (Social-only event).

An event EE is social-only if it contains no validated tokens:

SocialOnly⁡(E):⇔𝒯⁡(E)=∅.\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E)\;:\iff\;\mathcal{T}(E)=\emptyset.

Equivalently,

SocialOnly⁡(E):⇔¬∃⁡m∈E,∃τ∈𝒯⁡(HasTok⁡(m,τ)∧Valid⁡(τ)).\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E)\;:\iff\;\neg\exists m\in E,\ \exists\tau\in\mathcal{T}\;(\mathrm{HasTok}(m,\tau)\wedge\mathrm{Valid}(\tau)).
Remark 1 (Social-only vs. trigger-inactive).

Social-only refers strictly to token-emptiness: SocialOnly⁡(E)\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E) means 𝒯⁡(E)=∅\mathcal{T}(E)=\emptyset. Separately, for a given contract, a step is trigger-inactive if Jit=∅J_{i}^{t}=\emptyset (Definition 4). Under an evidential contract, SocialOnly⁡(Eit)\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E_{i}^{t}) implies Jit=∅J_{i}^{t}=\emptyset, but the converse need not hold (tokens may be present but fail to satisfy any preregistered trigger).

4 Preregistered Belief Revision Contracts

Semantic convention.

As in Section 3, each message event EE (a multiset of messages) induces a first-order structure 𝒮⁡(E)\mathcal{S}(E) over the public event/evidence signature. We write E⊧φE\models\varphi as shorthand for 𝒮⁡(E)⊧φ\mathcal{S}(E)\models\varphi.

Token notation.

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be the universe of tokens. For an event EE, define the candidate and validated token sets

𝒯all​(E):={τ∈𝒯:∃m∈E​HasTok​(m,τ)},𝒯⁡(E):={τ∈𝒯all​(E):Valid⁡(τ)}.\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{all}}(E)\;:=\;\{\tau\in\mathcal{T}:\exists m\in E\ \mathrm{HasTok}(m,\tau)\},\qquad\mathcal{T}(E)\;:=\;\{\tau\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{all}}(E):\mathrm{Valid}(\tau)\}.

For a step event EitE_{i}^{t}, we write 𝒯it:=𝒯⁡(Eit)\mathcal{T}_{i}^{t}:=\mathcal{T}(E_{i}^{t}).

4.1 Syntax

Definition 2 (Contract).

A PBRC contract for agent ii is a publicly preregistered tuple

Ci=⟨(φi,1,Ui,1),…,(φi,ki,Ui,ki),≺i,δi⟩C_{i}=\langle(\varphi_{i,1},U_{i,1}),\dots,(\varphi_{i,k_{i}},U_{i,k_{i}}),\prec_{i},\delta_{i}\rangle

where:

  1. 1.

    each trigger φi,j∈FO\varphi_{i,j}\in\mathrm{FO} is an event predicate evaluated on 𝒮⁡(E)\mathcal{S}(E) at runtime;

  2. 2.

    each Ui,jU_{i,j} is a (possibly partial) revision operator that maps a current belief state and the current event to a next belief state,

    Ui,j:Δ⁡(ℋ)×𝖤𝗏𝗍⇀Δ⁡(ℋ),U_{i,j}:\Delta(\mathcal{H})\times\mathsf{Evt}\ \rightharpoonup\ \Delta(\mathcal{H}),

    with 𝖤𝗏𝗍\mathsf{Evt} the set of events (multisets of messages);

  3. 3.

    ≺i\prec_{i} is a strict total priority order on {1,…,ki}\{1,\dots,k_{i}\} used to resolve multiple satisfied triggers (so the selected trigger index is unique);

  4. 4.

    δi\delta_{i} is a fallback operator used when no trigger is satisfied (or when enforcement rejects a proposed triggered update).

Definition 3 (Evidential contract).

A contract CiC_{i} is evidential if every trigger can fire only on non-social events, i.e.,

∀j,∀E,E⊧φi,j⟹𝒯⁡(E)≠∅.\forall j,\ \forall E,\quad E\models\varphi_{i,j}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathcal{T}(E)\neq\emptyset.

Equivalently (using SocialOnly⁡(E)⇔𝒯⁡(E)=∅\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E)\iff\mathcal{T}(E)=\emptyset),

∀j,∀E,E⊧φi,j⟹¬SocialOnly⁡(E).\forall j,\ \forall E,\quad E\models\varphi_{i,j}\ \Longrightarrow\ \neg\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E).
Remark 2 (Well-formedness).

To avoid undefined transitions, we assume contracts are well-formed in the sense that whenever a trigger is selected by the priority rule, the associated operator is defined for every belief and event on which it is selected, and fallback is total on all belief/event pairs. (If an implementation encounters an undefined operator at runtime, it must fall back and log the step as non-triggered.)

4.2 Contract-constrained update

Definition 4 (Trigger set and contract update).

Given belief bitb_{i}^{t} and event EitE_{i}^{t}, define the trigger set

Jit:={j∈{1,…,ki}:Eit⊧φi,j}.J_{i}^{t}:=\{j\in\{1,\dots,k_{i}\}:E_{i}^{t}\models\varphi_{i,j}\}.

The contract-constrained update is:

bit+1:={Ui,j⋆​(bit,Eit),if Jit≠∅,j⋆=min≺iJit,δi​(bit,Eit),if ​Jit=∅.b_{i}^{t+1}:=\begin{cases}U_{i,j^{\star}}(b_{i}^{t},E_{i}^{t}),&\text{if }J_{i}^{t}\neq\emptyset,\ j^{\star}=\min_{\prec_{i}}J_{i}^{t},\\ \delta_{i}(b_{i}^{t},E_{i}^{t}),&\text{if }J_{i}^{t}=\emptyset.\end{cases} (1)

4.3 Certificates and auditability

Definition 5 (Update certificate).

An abstract step certificate is a pair πit=(ℓit,Wit)\pi_{i}^{t}=(\ell_{i}^{t},W_{i}^{t}), with label ℓit∈{1,…,ki}∪{⊥}\ell_{i}^{t}\in\{1,\ldots,k_{i}\}\cup\{\bot\} and token set Wit⊆𝒯W_{i}^{t}\subseteq\mathcal{T}. Fallback is represented by (⊥,∅)(\bot,\emptyset). An accepted triggered step requires a nonempty validated witness, satisfaction of the named trigger on the full event, and selection of that trigger by the contract’s total priority order. Implementations may additionally carry a proof payload σ\sigma; for conjunctive existential triggers this is the variable assignment checked in Section 12. The pair notation projects away that payload and is not a claim that an unstructured set alone can be checked in linear time.

Definition 6 (Token-restricted satisfaction and witnesses).

For W⊆𝒯all​(E)W\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{\rm all}(E), let 𝒮W​(E)\mathcal{S}_{W}(E) restrict the event’s token domain and all token-dependent relations to WW, retaining the public context and non-token event relations. Define

E⊧Wφ⟺𝒮W(E)⊧φ.E\models_{W}\varphi\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathcal{S}_{W}(E)\models\varphi.

A witness for φ\varphi on EE is a set W⊆𝒯⁡(E)W\subseteq\mathcal{T}(E) such that E⊧WφE\models_{W}\varphi. A deterministic extractor for an evidential trigger must return such a nonempty set whenever the trigger is satisfied. Existence of an extractor is an additional contract requirement; it does not follow for arbitrary first-order formulas. For general trigger protocols, Definition 18 states the precise conditional requirement used by the translations.

A router checks (i) W≠∅W\neq\emptyset and current-event membership and validity, (ii) restricted satisfaction E⊧Wφi,ℓE\models_{W}\varphi_{i,\ell} using any required proof payload, (iii) full-event satisfaction E⊧φi,ℓE\models\varphi_{i,\ell}, and (iv) ℓ=min≺iJ(E)\ell=\min_{\prec_{i}}J(E). These are distinct checks. For nonmonotone formulas, restricting tokens can remove a counterexample, so restricted satisfaction need not imply full-event satisfaction. Conversely, a trigger that requires an invalid token need not admit a witness consisting only of validated tokens.

The definition is event-relative: sender-dependent or message-dependent predicates require the relevant event metadata during verification. A token-only verifier is justified only for the restricted class of Definition 19. A certificate licenses a transition under the specified policy; sole dependence on evidence content requires token invariance, and numerical operator compliance requires the enforcement regime below.

4.4 Enforcement semantics, trust boundary, and operator compliance

Certificates make belief revision auditable as an admissibility claim. A distinct trust boundary concerns operator compliance: even with a valid witness, can an agent output an arbitrary next belief/decision while claiming it applied Ui,j⋆U_{i,j^{\star}}? We therefore distinguish three enforcement architectures and state explicitly which results depend on which.

(A) Gate-only admissibility checking.

A minimal output gate verifies admissibility (e.g., W≠∅W\neq\emptyset, W⊆𝒯⁡(E)W\subseteq\mathcal{T}(E), and E⊧Wφi,ℓE\models_{W}\varphi_{i,\ell}) and then accepts or rejects an agent-supplied update. This supports checking admissibility of the certificate, but the numerical router-projection/normal-form results in Section 8.5 additionally require honest or verified operator execution. The gate does not, by itself, guarantee that an accepted numerical transition equals applying Ui,ℓU_{i,\ell} to the authoritative prior state unless agents are assumed honest with respect to operators.

(B) Proof-carrying updates (verifiable computation).

To enforce operator compliance without executing Ui,jU_{i,j} inside the router, the agent can attach a proof that its output equals Ui,j⋆​(bit,Eit)U_{i,j^{\star}}(b_{i}^{t},E_{i}^{t}) (or equals the contractually specified decision rule), in the spirit of proof-carrying mechanisms [Necula(1997)]. We treat this as an optional deployment path; our logical development does not depend on any specific proof system.

(C) State-holding routers (router-executed dynamics; default).

A practically common and conceptually clean architecture is a state-holding router that maintains the authoritative protocol state and executes the contract update itself. Concretely, the router stores bitb_{i}^{t}, validates tokens, checks triggers, extracts a witness, and then sets

bit+1:={Ui,j⋆​(bit,Eit),if a trigger j⋆ fires with a nonempty witness,δi​(bit,Eit),otherwise,b_{i}^{t+1}:=\begin{cases}U_{i,j^{\star}}(b_{i}^{t},E_{i}^{t}),&\text{if a trigger $j^{\star}$ fires with a nonempty witness},\\ \delta_{i}(b_{i}^{t},E_{i}^{t}),&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

while recording the corresponding certificate πit\pi_{i}^{t}. Unless stated otherwise, all results that reason about belief trajectories bitb_{i}^{t} are interpreted under this router-executed semantics. Gate-only checking (A) supports certificate-admissibility statements. Audit equivalence as defined below includes numerical beliefs and therefore also requires operator compliance. Rejections record the proposed certificate and rejection reason separately from the executed fallback label.

4.5 Protocol diagram

Figure 1 provides a round-level view of the PBRC enforcement pipeline: upon receiving an event EitE_{i}^{t}, the system validates candidate evidence tokens, checks preregistered triggers, and records an admissibility certificate πit=(j⋆,Wit)\pi_{i}^{t}=(j^{\star},W_{i}^{t}).

5 Running example: “peer pressure” misinformation triage

We use a minimal running example to illustrate three distinct phenomena that PBRC separates by construction: (i) purely social persuasion (rhetoric without validated evidence), (ii) evidence-gated belief revision (admissible changes of mind justified by tokens and witnesses), and (iii) the distinction between replay (stale-but-valid evidence) and forgery (manufactured “valid” evidence).

We will return to this example throughout the paper to ground the formal results. Specifically, we will show how the social-only guarantees (Section 6) prevent the cascade described in Section 5.2, how the normal form representation (Section 8) canonicalizes the evidence-gated revision in Section 5.3, and how the adversary models (Section 9) formalize the replay and forgery attacks in Section 5.4.

5.1 Setup

Let ℋ={True,False}\mathcal{H}=\{\textsf{True},\textsf{False}\} encode whether a concrete news claim is true or false. Agent ii maintains a belief distribution bit∈Δ⁡(ℋ)b_{i}^{t}\in\Delta(\mathcal{H}). Suppose the initial belief is moderately confident in truth:

bi0​(True)=0.6,bi0​(False)=0.4.b_{i}^{0}(\textsf{True})=0.6,\qquad b_{i}^{0}(\textsf{False})=0.4.

Tokens represent externally checkable evidence artifacts (e.g., signed tool outputs or retrieval receipts) and are validated by the system’s validity layer. For an event EE (a multiset of received messages), let 𝒯⁡(E)\mathcal{T}(E) denote its set of valid tokens; SocialOnly⁡(E)\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E) is equivalent to 𝒯⁡(E)=∅\mathcal{T}(E)=\emptyset.

Agent ii preregisters a simple evidential contract with two prioritized triggers:

  1. 1.

    Verified falsifier (high priority). There exists a valid token contradicting True:

    φ1:=∃τ⁡(Valid⁡(τ)∧Contradicts⁡(τ,True)).\varphi_{1}\;:=\;\exists\tau\ \big(\mathrm{Valid}(\tau)\wedge\mathrm{Contradicts}(\tau,\textsf{True})\big).
  2. 2.

    Verified support. There exists a valid token supporting True:

    φ2:=∃τ⁡(Valid⁡(τ)∧Supports⁡(τ,True)).\varphi_{2}\;:=\;\exists\tau\ \big(\mathrm{Valid}(\tau)\wedge\mathrm{Supports}(\tau,\textsf{True})\big).

The priority order is φ1≺φ2\varphi_{1}\prec\varphi_{2}. When no trigger is admissibly fired, the fallback is skeptical dilution δλ\delta_{\lambda} (Definition 8).

For a complete numerical example take λ=0.1\lambda=0.1. Writing p=b⁡(True)p=b(\textsf{True}), define U1U_{1} by p′=p/(p+4​(1−p))p^{\prime}=p/(p+4(1-p)) and U2U_{2} by p′=4​p/(4​p+1−p)p^{\prime}=4p/(4p+1-p), with complementary mass on False. These are fixed bounded log-odds changes on interior beliefs and well-defined at the endpoints. Assume a sound and complete state-holding router verifies the selected witness and computes these updates (Section 8.5).

5.2 Outcome under purely social persuasion (token-empty round)

At round t=0t=0, a peer sends a confident message such as “Everyone agrees it is False.” Crucially, the message contains no validated citations or tool outputs; formally, the received event Ei0E_{i}^{0} is social-only:

SocialOnly(Ei0)⟺𝒯(Ei0)=∅.\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E_{i}^{0})\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathcal{T}(E_{i}^{0})=\emptyset.

Because the contract is evidential, neither φ1\varphi_{1} nor φ2\varphi_{2} can hold on a token-empty event, hence Ji0=∅J_{i}^{0}=\emptyset and the enforced update is necessarily fallback:

bi1=δλ​(bi0,Ei0).b_{i}^{1}\;=\;\delta_{\lambda}(b_{i}^{0},E_{i}^{0}).

By Theorem 1, confidence cannot increase in such a round, and by Lemma 2 the top hypothesis is preserved. In particular, the peer’s rhetoric cannot flip the decision from True to False without validated evidence, even if the rhetoric is unanimous, prestigious, or highly confident.

5.3 Outcome with a valid evidence token (auditable flip)

Suppose at a later round a peer provides a validated citation token τ⋆\tau^{\star} (e.g., a retrieval-verified snippet or a signed fact-check result) such that

Valid⁡(τ⋆)andContradicts⁡(τ⋆,True).\mathrm{Valid}(\tau^{\star})\quad\text{and}\quad\mathrm{Contradicts}(\tau^{\star},\textsf{True}).

Then Ei1E_{i}^{1} is non-social and satisfies φ1\varphi_{1}, so the highest-priority trigger fires. Under enforcement, the update is accepted only if it is justified by a nonempty witness set; here a natural witness is Wi1={τ⋆}W_{i}^{1}=\{\tau^{\star}\}. After the first fallback, bi1​(True)=0.59b_{i}^{1}(\textsf{True})=0.59. Applying U1U_{1} gives bi2​(True)=0.59/(0.59+4⋅0.41)≈0.265b_{i}^{2}(\textsf{True})=0.59/(0.59+4\cdot 0.41)\approx 0.265, so the top changes to False. The certificate records the selected license (Theorem 17); correctness of the new answer still depends on the evidence and operator assumptions.

5.4 Replay versus forgery (preview)

This example also clarifies two orthogonal integrity threats.

Replay. A peer may retransmit an old token τ⋆\tau^{\star} that was once valid but is no longer contextually applicable (e.g., wrong claim instance, stale timestamp, or mismatched retrieval context). If Valid⁡(τ)\mathrm{Valid}(\tau) does not bind tokens to an instance identifier and a freshness condition, then replayed evidence can satisfy φ1\varphi_{1} despite being irrelevant. This is addressed by freshness/context predicates inside triggers (Section 9), e.g., requiring FreshΔ\mathrm{Fresh}_{\Delta} and/or an instance hash match as part of admissibility.

Forgery. If an adversary can fabricate tokens that pass Valid\mathrm{Valid} (e.g., by compromising validators or the verification channel), then it can manufacture admissible “evidence” for arbitrary conclusions. If the forged certificate passes all full-event and priority checks, is accepted, and its selected operator produces an adverse output at the current belief, that output occurs (Theorem 19). Forgeability alone does not imply that any chosen contract can be forced to flip. Integrity, applicability, operator design, and faithful execution all remain relevant.

6 Main guarantees (theorem-centric)

This section establishes the core social-dynamics guarantees of PBRC. The central theme is that, under evidential contracts and conservative fallback, purely social interaction cannot (i) increase confidence or (ii) induce a new high-confidence wrong consensus.

To orient the reader, we proceed in four steps. First, we define the necessary properties of fallback operators (Section 6.1). Second, we prove that in token-empty (social-only) rounds, confidence cannot increase (Section 6.2). Third, we establish the central impossibility result: purely conformity-driven cascades cannot occur under PBRC (Section 6.3). Finally, we provide a minimal topology statement showing why identical admitted evidence yields identical beliefs under an evidence-additive policy (Section 6.4). These formal results directly explain the cascade suppression observed in the misinformation triage example (Section 5).

6.1 Fallback operators and skeptical dilution

Definition 7 (Argmax-preserving and non-amplifying fallback).

Fix a confidence functional conf:Δ⁡(ℋ)→ℝ\mathrm{conf}:\Delta(\mathcal{H})\to\mathbb{R} (in the main text we take conf⁡(b)=maxh∈ℋ⁡b⁡(h)\mathrm{conf}(b)=\max_{h\in\mathcal{H}}b(h)). A fallback operator δi:Δ⁡(ℋ)×𝔼​v→Δ⁡(ℋ)\delta_{i}:\Delta(\mathcal{H})\times\mathbb{E}\mathrm{v}\to\Delta(\mathcal{H}) is:

  1. 1.

    argmax-preserving if argmax⁡(δi​(b,E))=argmax⁡(b)\mathrm{argmax}(\delta_{i}(b,E))=\mathrm{argmax}(b) for all b,Eb,E;

  2. 2.

    non-amplifying if conf⁡(δi​(b,E))≤conf⁡(b)\mathrm{conf}(\delta_{i}(b,E))\leq\mathrm{conf}(b) for all b,Eb,E.

Definition 8 (Skeptical dilution).

Fix λ∈[0,1)\lambda\in[0,1) and let uu denote the uniform distribution on ℋ\mathcal{H}. Define the skeptical-dilution fallback

δλ​(b,E):=(1−λ)​b+λ​u.\delta_{\lambda}(b,E)\ :=\ (1-\lambda)b+\lambda u.
Lemma 1 (Closed form under repeated skeptical dilution).

Let b0∈Δ⁡(ℋ)b^{0}\in\Delta(\mathcal{H}) and define bt+1=δλ​(bt,Et)b^{t+1}=\delta_{\lambda}(b^{t},E^{t}) for an arbitrary sequence of events (Et)t≥0(E^{t})_{t\geq 0}. Then for all t≥0t\geq 0,

bt=(1−λ)t​b0+(1−(1−λ)t)​u,b^{t}=(1-\lambda)^{t}\,b^{0}+\bigl(1-(1-\lambda)^{t}\bigr)\,u,

and, writing TV⁡(p,q)=12​‖p−q‖1\mathrm{TV}(p,q)=\tfrac{1}{2}\|p-q\|_{1} for total variation distance,

TV⁡(bt,u)=(1−λ)t​TV​(b0,u).\mathrm{TV}(b^{t},u)=(1-\lambda)^{t}\,\mathrm{TV}(b^{0},u).
Proof.

By Definition 8,

bt+1=(1−λ)​bt+λ​u.b^{t+1}=(1-\lambda)b^{t}+\lambda u.

Iterating the affine recursion yields bt=(1−λ)t​b0+(1−(1−λ)t)​ub^{t}=(1-\lambda)^{t}b^{0}+\bigl(1-(1-\lambda)^{t}\bigr)u. Subtracting uu gives bt−u=(1−λ)t​(b0−u)b^{t}-u=(1-\lambda)^{t}(b^{0}-u), and taking TV(⋅,u)=12∥⋅−u∥1\mathrm{TV}(\cdot,u)=\tfrac{1}{2}\|\cdot-u\|_{1} pulls out the constant factor (1−λ)t(1-\lambda)^{t}. ∎

Lemma 2 (Skeptical dilution preserves argmax and does not amplify confidence).

For any λ∈[0,1)\lambda\in[0,1), δλ\delta_{\lambda} is argmax-preserving and non-amplifying in the sense of Definition 7. Moreover, if λ>0\lambda>0 and bb is not uniform (equivalently, conf⁡(b)>1/|ℋ|\mathrm{conf}(b)>1/|\mathcal{H}|), then conf⁡(δλ​(b,E))<conf⁡(b)\mathrm{conf}(\delta_{\lambda}(b,E))<\mathrm{conf}(b).

Proof.

For any h,h′∈ℋh,h^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H},

δλ​(b,E)​(h)−δλ​(b,E)​(h′)=(1−λ)​(b⁡(h)−b⁡(h′)),\delta_{\lambda}(b,E)(h)-\delta_{\lambda}(b,E)(h^{\prime})=(1-\lambda)\bigl(b(h)-b(h^{\prime})\bigr),

so strict inequalities and equalities among coordinates are preserved; hence the entire argmax\mathrm{argmax} set is preserved.

For confidence, let m=conf⁡(b)=maxh⁡b⁡(h)m=\mathrm{conf}(b)=\max_{h}b(h). Then

conf⁡(δλ​(b,E))=maxh⁡((1−λ)​b​(h)+λ/|ℋ|)=(1−λ)​m+λ/|ℋ|≤m,\mathrm{conf}(\delta_{\lambda}(b,E))=\max_{h}\Bigl((1-\lambda)b(h)+\lambda/|\mathcal{H}|\Bigr)=(1-\lambda)m+\lambda/|\mathcal{H}|\leq m,

since m≥1/|ℋ|m\geq 1/|\mathcal{H}| for any distribution. Strictness holds exactly when λ>0\lambda>0 and m>1/|ℋ|m>1/|\mathcal{H}|. At λ=0\lambda=0 the operator is the identity. The proofs use exact arithmetic; finite precision needs an explicit tie policy, and λ=1\lambda=1 is excluded because it can introduce new maximizers. ∎

6.2 Token-empty rounds and social non-amplification

Recall that SocialOnly⁡(E)\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E) means EE contains no valid tokens, i.e. 𝒯⁡(E)=∅\mathcal{T}(E)=\emptyset.

Definition 9 (Trigger-inactive round).

Round tt is trigger-inactive for agent ii if Jit=∅J_{i}^{t}=\emptyset, i.e., no preregistered trigger is satisfied at that step and the intended contract update is fallback.

Remark 3 (Token-empty implies trigger-inactive under evidential contracts).

If agent ii uses an evidential contract (every trigger implies ¬SocialOnly\neg\mathrm{SocialOnly}), then SocialOnly⁡(Eit)\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E_{i}^{t}) implies Jit=∅J_{i}^{t}=\emptyset at round tt. Under enforcement regimes (B) or (C) with empty-witness rejection, such token-empty rounds are therefore necessarily enforced as fallback steps.

Theorem 1 (Social non-amplification).

If δi\delta_{i} is non-amplifying, then for any agent ii and any trigger-inactive round tt (Definition 9),

conf⁡(bit+1)≤conf⁡(bit).\mathrm{conf}(b_{i}^{t+1})\leq\mathrm{conf}(b_{i}^{t}).

If, moreover, δi=δλ\delta_{i}=\delta_{\lambda} with 0<λ<10<\lambda<1 and bitb_{i}^{t} is non-uniform, then the inequality is strict.

Proof.

If round tt is trigger-inactive for agent ii, then by the one-step update semantics (Equation (1)) we have bit+1=δi​(bit,Eit)b_{i}^{t+1}=\delta_{i}(b_{i}^{t},E_{i}^{t}). Non-amplification of δi\delta_{i} gives conf⁡(bit+1)≤conf⁡(bit)\mathrm{conf}(b_{i}^{t+1})\leq\mathrm{conf}(b_{i}^{t}). If δi=δλ\delta_{i}=\delta_{\lambda} with 0<λ<10<\lambda<1 and bitb_{i}^{t} is non-uniform, strictness follows from Lemma 2. ∎

Corollary 1 (Convergence to maximal uncertainty under repeated trigger-inactive rounds).

Assume CiC_{i} is evidential and δi=δλ\delta_{i}=\delta_{\lambda} with 0<λ<10<\lambda<1. If rounds 0,1,…,T−10,1,\dots,T-1 are trigger-inactive for agent ii, then

biT=(1−λ)T​bi0+(1−(1−λ)T)​u,TV⁡(biT,u)=(1−λ)T​TV​(bi0,u).b_{i}^{T}=(1-\lambda)^{T}b_{i}^{0}+\bigl(1-(1-\lambda)^{T}\bigr)u,\qquad\mathrm{TV}(b_{i}^{T},u)=(1-\lambda)^{T}\mathrm{TV}(b_{i}^{0},u).
Proof.

Under the hypothesis, bit+1=δλ​(bit,Eit)b_{i}^{t+1}=\delta_{\lambda}(b_{i}^{t},E_{i}^{t}) for all t<Tt<T. Apply Lemma 1. Since 0<1−λ<10<1-\lambda<1, the displayed distance tends to zero if the inactive interval continues indefinitely. ∎

6.3 Impossibility of purely conformity-driven wrong-but-sure cascades

The most dangerous failure mode in deliberative systems is a “wrong-but-sure” cascade: the population converges to a high-confidence consensus on an incorrect hypothesis, driven entirely by mutual reinforcement rather than evidence. The running example shows how the contract blocks a token-empty top change; the pooling baseline in Section 13.2 illustrates population amplification. We analyze fallback-only intervals, a class that includes token-empty intervals under evidential enforcement but may also contain rejected evidence-bearing steps.

Fix a designated true hypothesis h⋆∈ℋh^{\star}\in\mathcal{H} and a confidence threshold γ∈(1/|ℋ|,1]\gamma\in(1/|\mathcal{H}|,1].

Definition 10 (Social-driven wrong-but-sure cascade).

A social-driven wrong-but-sure cascade to a false hypothesis h≠h⋆h\neq h^{\star} occurs over an interval [t0,t1][t_{0},t_{1}] if:

  1. 1.

    (fallback-only interval) for every agent ii and every round t∈{t0,…,t1−1}t\in\{t_{0},\dots,t_{1}-1\}, the executed update is fallback; and

  2. 2.

    (wrong but sure at the end) for every agent ii, argmax⁡(bit1)={h}\mathrm{argmax}(b_{i}^{t_{1}})=\{h\} and conf⁡(bit1)≥γ\mathrm{conf}(b_{i}^{t_{1}})\geq\gamma.

Theorem 2 (No social-driven cascades under argmax-preserving fallback).

Assume each agent ii uses a fallback δi\delta_{i} that is argmax-preserving and non-amplifying (Definition 7). If rounds t0,…,t1−1t_{0},\dots,t_{1}-1 are trigger-inactive for all agents, then for every agent ii,

argmax⁡(bit1)=argmax⁡(bit0),conf⁡(bit1)≤conf⁡(bit0).\mathrm{argmax}(b_{i}^{t_{1}})=\mathrm{argmax}(b_{i}^{t_{0}}),\qquad\mathrm{conf}(b_{i}^{t_{1}})\leq\mathrm{conf}(b_{i}^{t_{0}}).

Consequently, no social-driven wrong-but-sure cascade (Definition 10) can occur unless it already held at time t0t_{0}.

Proof.

Fix an agent ii. Since rounds t0,…,t1−1t_{0},\dots,t_{1}-1 are trigger-inactive for ii, we have bit+1=δi​(bit,Eit)b_{i}^{t+1}=\delta_{i}(b_{i}^{t},E_{i}^{t}) for all t0≤t<t1t_{0}\leq t<t_{1}. Argmax-preservation yields argmax⁡(bit+1)=argmax⁡(bit)\mathrm{argmax}(b_{i}^{t+1})=\mathrm{argmax}(b_{i}^{t}) at each step, hence argmax⁡(bit1)=argmax⁡(bit0)\mathrm{argmax}(b_{i}^{t_{1}})=\mathrm{argmax}(b_{i}^{t_{0}}) by iteration. Non-amplification yields conf⁡(bit+1)≤conf⁡(bit)\mathrm{conf}(b_{i}^{t+1})\leq\mathrm{conf}(b_{i}^{t}) at each step, hence conf⁡(bit1)≤conf⁡(bit0)\mathrm{conf}(b_{i}^{t_{1}})\leq\mathrm{conf}(b_{i}^{t_{0}}) by iteration. ∎

6.4 A minimal topology statement under evidence closure

The detailed topology-to-trace factorization results appear later (Sections 8–8.5.4). For completeness, we record here a simple “closure implies topology-irrelevance” principle for policies whose epistemic state is a function of admitted evidence sets.

Definition 11 (Evidence closure).

Let 𝒦<T\mathcal{K}^{<T} denote the set of all valid tokens that appear anywhere in the system before time TT:

𝒦<T:=⋃i∈𝒜⋃t<T𝒯⁡(Eit).\mathcal{K}^{<T}\ :=\ \bigcup_{i\in\mathcal{A}}\ \bigcup_{t<T}\ \mathcal{T}(E_{i}^{t}).

A run achieves evidence closure by time TT if every agent has access to every such token at time TT:

∀i∈𝒜,𝒦<T⊆𝒦iT,\forall i\in\mathcal{A},\quad\mathcal{K}^{<T}\ \subseteq\ \mathcal{K}_{i}^{T},

where 𝒦iT\mathcal{K}_{i}^{T} denotes the set of valid tokens available to agent ii after processing rounds 0,…,T−10,\dots,T-1 (e.g., 𝒦iT=⋃t<T𝒯⁡(Eit)\mathcal{K}_{i}^{T}=\bigcup_{t<T}\mathcal{T}(E_{i}^{t}), or with an explicit initial set if present).

Definition 12 (Evidence-additive revision).

A revision policy for agent ii is evidence-additive if there exists a function FiF_{i} and an “admission” map Admit\mathrm{Admit} such that

bit=Fi​(𝒮it),𝒮it+1=𝒮it∪Admit⁡(Ci,Eit),b_{i}^{t}=F_{i}(\mathcal{S}_{i}^{t}),\qquad\mathcal{S}_{i}^{t+1}=\mathcal{S}_{i}^{t}\cup\mathrm{Admit}(C_{i},E_{i}^{t}),

where 𝒮it\mathcal{S}_{i}^{t} is the cumulative set of admitted tokens up to time tt, and Admit⁡(Ci,Eit)⊆𝒯⁡(Eit)\mathrm{Admit}(C_{i},E_{i}^{t})\subseteq\mathcal{T}(E_{i}^{t}) is a (possibly empty) witness set used to justify admissible revision at round tt.

Definition 13 (Sender-invariant triggers).

Fix a receiver ii. A trigger χ\chi is sender-invariant if its satisfaction depends only on token-level facts available at ii (e.g., Valid\mathrm{Valid}, Supports\mathrm{Supports}, Contradicts\mathrm{Contradicts}, token types, and freshness predicates), and not on the identities of message senders except insofar as those identities are explicitly bound into tokens. Equivalently, χ\chi is definable in the token-only signature obtained by removing Send\mathrm{Send} and other non-token message metadata.

Theorem 3 (Topology irrelevance given identical admitted evidence sets).

Assume agent ii uses evidence-additive revision (Definition 12) and all triggers are sender-invariant (Definition 13). Consider two runs (possibly on different topologies and with different message orderings/rhetoric) that induce the same admitted evidence set at time TT, i.e. 𝒮iT\mathcal{S}_{i}^{T} is identical in both runs. Then the terminal belief is identical: biTb_{i}^{T} is the same in both runs. In particular, under evidence closure (Definition 11), any topology/order/rhetoric variation that does not change 𝒮iT\mathcal{S}_{i}^{T} cannot change biTb_{i}^{T}.

Proof.

By evidence-additivity, biT=Fi​(𝒮iT)b_{i}^{T}=F_{i}(\mathcal{S}_{i}^{T}). If 𝒮iT\mathcal{S}_{i}^{T} is the same across the two runs, then the right-hand side is the same, hence biTb_{i}^{T} is the same. Sender-invariance is included to emphasize that admissibility judgments can be designed to depend only on token-level evidence rather than social metadata; the stronger token-sufficiency and topology-to-trace results later make this dependence precise. ∎

7 Minimality and necessity results

This section formalizes a class of auditable trigger protocols and characterizes their behavior under evidence-free (social-only) interaction. Fallback constraints apply only where fallback can be selected; trigger constraints apply to the actual selected transition. The results are intentionally elementary: they are “one-step” necessity statements that isolate which part of a protocol must carry the burden of social robustness.

We structure this analysis as follows. First, we define the general class of auditable trigger protocols (Section 7.1). Second, we formalize evidence-free robustness properties (Section 7.2). Third, we prove that fallback operators must be conservative to satisfy these properties (Section 7.3). Finally, we characterize robustness through every selected social-only transition and show why syntactic evidence gating is sufficient but not necessary (Section 7.4).

7.1 Auditable trigger protocols

Definition 14 (Auditable trigger protocol).

Fix an agent ii and hypothesis space ℋ\mathcal{H}. An auditable trigger protocol for agent ii is a tuple

Pi=⟨(ψi,1,Vi,1),…,(ψi,ri,Vi,ri),≺i,δi⟩P_{i}=\langle(\psi_{i,1},V_{i,1}),\dots,(\psi_{i,r_{i}},V_{i,r_{i}}),\prec_{i},\delta_{i}\rangle

where: (i) each ψi,j\psi_{i,j} is a public predicate over events EE (a trigger); (ii) each Vi,j:Δ⁡(ℋ)×𝔼​v→Δ⁡(ℋ)V_{i,j}:\Delta(\mathcal{H})\times\mathbb{E}\mathrm{v}\to\Delta(\mathcal{H}) is an update operator; (iii) ≺i\prec_{i} is a strict total priority order on {1,…,ri}\{1,\dots,r_{i}\}; (iv) δi:Δ⁡(ℋ)×𝔼​v→Δ⁡(ℋ)\delta_{i}:\Delta(\mathcal{H})\times\mathbb{E}\mathrm{v}\to\Delta(\mathcal{H}) is a fallback operator. On input (b,E)(b,E) the protocol selects the highest-priority satisfied trigger (if any) and applies its operator; otherwise it applies fallback:

FPi(b,E)={Vi,j⋆​(b,E),JPi​(E)≠∅,δi​(b,E),JPi​(E)=∅,j⋆=min≺iJPi(E),F_{P_{i}}(b,E)=\begin{cases}V_{i,j^{\star}}(b,E),&J_{P_{i}}(E)\neq\emptyset,\\ \delta_{i}(b,E),&J_{P_{i}}(E)=\emptyset,\end{cases}\qquad j^{\star}=\min_{\prec_{i}}J_{P_{i}}(E),

where JPi​(E):={j:E⊧ψi,j}J_{P_{i}}(E):=\{j:E\models\psi_{i,j}\}.

Remark 4 (When necessity statements are non-vacuous).

Theorems 4 and 5 only constrain δi\delta_{i} on social-only inputs that can actually reach fallback, i.e., on social-only events EE such that JPi​(E)=∅J_{P_{i}}(E)=\emptyset for the relevant run. We state the conditions explicitly below to avoid vacuity.

7.2 Evidence-free robustness properties

Recall that SocialOnly⁡(E)\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E) means EE contains no valid evidence tokens (equivalently, 𝒯⁡(E)=∅\mathcal{T}(E)=\emptyset).

Definition 15 (Evidence-free peer-pressure immunity).

A protocol PiP_{i} has evidence-free peer-pressure immunity if for every initial belief bi0∈Δ⁡(ℋ)b_{i}^{0}\in\Delta(\mathcal{H}) and every event stream (Et)t≥0(E^{t})_{t\geq 0} with SocialOnly⁡(Et)\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E^{t}) for all tt, the induced belief trajectory (bit)t≥0(b_{i}^{t})_{t\geq 0} satisfies

argmax⁡(bit)=argmax⁡(bi0)for all ​t≥0.\mathrm{argmax}(b_{i}^{t})=\mathrm{argmax}(b_{i}^{0})\quad\text{for all }t\geq 0.
Definition 16 (Evidence-free non-amplification).

Fix a confidence functional conf:Δ⁡(ℋ)→ℝ\mathrm{conf}:\Delta(\mathcal{H})\to\mathbb{R} (e.g., conf⁡(b)=maxh∈ℋ⁡b⁡(h)\mathrm{conf}(b)=\max_{h\in\mathcal{H}}b(h)). A protocol PiP_{i} has evidence-free non-amplification if for every initial belief bi0∈Δ⁡(ℋ)b_{i}^{0}\in\Delta(\mathcal{H}) and every event stream (Et)t≥0(E^{t})_{t\geq 0} with SocialOnly⁡(Et)\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E^{t}) for all tt, the induced belief trajectory satisfies

conf⁡(bit+1)≤conf⁡(bit)for all ​t≥0.\mathrm{conf}(b_{i}^{t+1})\leq\mathrm{conf}(b_{i}^{t})\quad\text{for all }t\geq 0.

7.3 Fallback minimality

Theorem 4 (Argmax-preserving fallback is necessary).

Let PiP_{i} be an auditable trigger protocol with evidence-free peer-pressure immunity (Definition 15). Assume there exists a social-only event EE such that JPi​(E)=∅J_{P_{i}}(E)=\emptyset (so fallback can be reached on a social-only input). Then δi\delta_{i} must be argmax-preserving on every social-only (b,E)(b,E) with JPi​(E)=∅J_{P_{i}}(E)=\emptyset:

∀b∈Δ⁡(ℋ)​∀E,(SocialOnly⁡(E)∧JPi​(E)=∅)⇒argmax⁡(δi​(b,E))=argmax⁡(b).\forall b\in\Delta(\mathcal{H})\ \forall E,\quad\big(\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E)\ \land\ J_{P_{i}}(E)=\emptyset\big)\Rightarrow\mathrm{argmax}(\delta_{i}(b,E))=\mathrm{argmax}(b).
Proof.

Suppose for contradiction that there exist bb and a social-only event EE with JPi​(E)=∅J_{P_{i}}(E)=\emptyset such that argmax⁡(δi​(b,E))≠argmax⁡(b)\mathrm{argmax}(\delta_{i}(b,E))\neq\mathrm{argmax}(b). Consider the length-one social-only run with initial belief bi0=bb_{i}^{0}=b and first event E0=EE^{0}=E. Because JPi​(E0)=∅J_{P_{i}}(E^{0})=\emptyset, the protocol applies fallback at t=0t=0, so bi1=δi​(bi0,E0)=δi​(b,E)b_{i}^{1}=\delta_{i}(b_{i}^{0},E^{0})=\delta_{i}(b,E). By construction argmax⁡(bi1)≠argmax⁡(bi0)\mathrm{argmax}(b_{i}^{1})\neq\mathrm{argmax}(b_{i}^{0}), contradicting evidence-free peer-pressure immunity. ∎

Theorem 5 (Non-amplifying fallback is necessary).

Let PiP_{i} be an auditable trigger protocol with evidence-free non-amplification (Definition 16). Assume there exists a social-only event EE such that JPi​(E)=∅J_{P_{i}}(E)=\emptyset. Then δi\delta_{i} must be non-amplifying on every social-only (b,E)(b,E) with JPi​(E)=∅J_{P_{i}}(E)=\emptyset:

∀b∈Δ⁡(ℋ)​∀E,(SocialOnly⁡(E)∧JPi​(E)=∅)⇒conf⁡(δi​(b,E))≤conf⁡(b).\forall b\in\Delta(\mathcal{H})\ \forall E,\quad\big(\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E)\ \land\ J_{P_{i}}(E)=\emptyset\big)\Rightarrow\mathrm{conf}(\delta_{i}(b,E))\leq\mathrm{conf}(b).
Proof.

Suppose for contradiction that there exist bb and a social-only event EE with JPi​(E)=∅J_{P_{i}}(E)=\emptyset such that conf⁡(δi​(b,E))>conf⁡(b)\mathrm{conf}(\delta_{i}(b,E))>\mathrm{conf}(b). Consider the length-one social-only run with bi0=bb_{i}^{0}=b and E0=EE^{0}=E. As above, fallback applies at t=0t=0, so bi1=δi​(b,E)b_{i}^{1}=\delta_{i}(b,E), hence conf⁡(bi1)>conf⁡(bi0)\mathrm{conf}(b_{i}^{1})>\mathrm{conf}(b_{i}^{0}), contradicting evidence-free non-amplification. ∎

7.4 Local characterization and the role of evidence gating

Definition 17 (Nontrivial revision operator).

An operator VV is nontrivial if for some (b,E)(b,E) it changes the top set or the confidence functional. This existential property makes no claim about its effect on a particular social-only input or about whether its trigger is ever selected.

Theorem 6 (Local characterization of social-only robustness).

Let FPiF_{P_{i}} be the actually selected deterministic transition of a trigger protocol, including fallback. Evidence-free peer-pressure immunity for all initial beliefs holds if and only if

∀b,E:SocialOnly⁡(E)⟹argmax⁡(FPi​(b,E))=argmax⁡(b).\forall b,E:\quad\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E)\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathrm{argmax}(F_{P_{i}}(b,E))=\mathrm{argmax}(b).

Evidence-free nonamplification holds if and only if

∀b,E:SocialOnly⁡(E)⟹conf⁡(FPi​(b,E))≤conf⁡(b).\forall b,E:\quad\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E)\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathrm{conf}(F_{P_{i}}(b,E))\leq\mathrm{conf}(b).
Proof.

For necessity choose the one-step social-only run initialized at the specified bb and receiving EE. The desired run property implies the local condition. For sufficiency apply the local condition at each step of an arbitrary social-only stream; induction preserves the initial top set, and the confidence inequalities hold consecutively. ∎

Example 1 (Why evidence gating is not a necessary syntactic condition).

A sole always-true trigger with operator V⁡(b,E)=(1−λ)​b+λ​uV(b,E)=(1-\lambda)b+\lambda u, 0<λ<10<\lambda<1, preserves the full top set and never increases maximum confidence, including on token-empty events. It is nevertheless nontrivial: for b=(0.8,0.2)b=(0.8,0.2) and λ=0.5\lambda=0.5, it returns (0.65,0.35)(0.65,0.35). Thus robust protocols can have nontrivial triggers satisfied by social-only events. A lower-priority trigger that is never selected is likewise unconstrained by an immunity property of realized transitions.

Remark 5 (Stability, confidence, and calibration).

Theorems 4–6 constrain actual selected transitions on social-only inputs. Evidence gating plus conservative fallback is one sufficient implementation of these conditions. Maximum-confidence nonamplification is not statistical calibration, and does not establish improved accuracy or a better proper scoring rule.

8 PBRC normal form, equivalence notions, and representation

The local characterization in Section 7 constrains behavior, not a unique syntax. We now distinguish two transformations. A behavior-preserving normal form moves the original social-only behavior into fallback; it preserves trajectories but need not make an unsafe protocol safe. Evidence-gated enforcement instead retains the original fallback and can suppress social-only triggered behavior. The results below assume the specified witness extractors exist and that original trigger predicates are expressible in the target contract language. For FO contracts, the original triggers are therefore assumed FO-definable.

We compare numerical trajectories and projected certificate traces. Canonicalizing an empty witness to the fallback label is a mathematical projection of the audit record, not an instruction to delete an agent’s original proposal or to certify that an arbitrary ungated social transition was conservative. Complete logs retain proposals, decisions, and actual updates.

8.1 One-step semantics of trigger protocols

Fix an agent ii and an auditable trigger protocol

Pi=⟨(ψi,1,Vi,1),…,(ψi,ri,Vi,ri),≺i,δi⟩,P_{i}=\langle(\psi_{i,1},V_{i,1}),\dots,(\psi_{i,r_{i}},V_{i,r_{i}}),\prec_{i},\delta_{i}\rangle,

where each ψi,j\psi_{i,j} is an event predicate (trigger), each Vi,jV_{i,j} is an update operator, δi\delta_{i} is the fallback, and ≺i\prec_{i} is a strict total priority order.11 1 For determinism we assume ≺i\prec_{i} is a strict total order on {1,…,ri}\{1,\dots,r_{i}\}. If priorities are specified only partially, fix any public tie-breaking refinement to a strict total order.

Given a belief state b∈Δ⁡(ℋ)b\in\Delta(\mathcal{H}) and an event EE, define the set of satisfied triggers:

JPi​(E):={j∈{1,…,ri}:E⊧ψi,j},jPi⋆​(E):={min≺iJPi(E),JPi​(E)≠∅,undefined,JPi​(E)=∅.J_{P_{i}}(E):=\{j\in\{1,\dots,r_{i}\}:E\models\psi_{i,j}\},\qquad j^{\star}_{P_{i}}(E):=\begin{cases}\min_{\prec_{i}}J_{P_{i}}(E),&J_{P_{i}}(E)\neq\emptyset,\\ \text{undefined},&J_{P_{i}}(E)=\emptyset.\end{cases}

The one-step belief update induced by PiP_{i} is

FPi​(b,E):={Vi,jPi⋆​(E)​(b,E),JPi​(E)≠∅,δi​(b,E),JPi​(E)=∅.F_{P_{i}}(b,E):=\begin{cases}V_{i,j^{\star}_{P_{i}}(E)}(b,E),&J_{P_{i}}(E)\neq\emptyset,\\ \delta_{i}(b,E),&J_{P_{i}}(E)=\emptyset.\end{cases} (2)

8.2 Two notions of equivalence: belief trajectories vs. audit traces

Validated tokens and social-only events.

For any event EE (multiset of messages), define the set of validated tokens contained in EE:

𝒯⁡(E):={τ∈𝒯:∃m∈E⁡(HasTok⁡(m,τ)∧Valid⁡(τ))}.\mathcal{T}(E)\;:=\;\{\tau\in\mathcal{T}:\exists m\in E\ (\mathrm{HasTok}(m,\tau)\wedge\mathrm{Valid}(\tau))\}.

By definition, SocialOnly⁡(E)\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E) holds iff 𝒯⁡(E)=∅\mathcal{T}(E)=\emptyset.

Witness extraction and token-witnessability.

To speak meaningfully about certificates, we assume that triggers are designed so that, whenever they hold in a non-social event, their satisfaction can be justified by exhibiting a concrete (nonempty) set of validated tokens.

Definition 18 (Witness extractor for a trigger protocol).

An extractor Witχ\mathrm{Wit}_{\chi} is a deterministic token-selection map such that, for every event EE:

  1. 1.

    Witχ​(E)⊆𝒯⁡(E)\mathrm{Wit}_{\chi}(E)\subseteq\mathcal{T}(E) (token soundness);

  2. 2.

    if E⊧χE\models\chi and 𝒯⁡(E)≠∅\mathcal{T}(E)\neq\emptyset, then Witχ​(E)≠∅\mathrm{Wit}_{\chi}(E)\neq\emptyset (nonvacuity);

  3. 3.

    under that same condition, E⊧Witχ​(E)χE\models_{\mathrm{Wit}_{\chi}(E)}\chi (witness correctness).

On token-empty events the map returns ∅\emptyset; no semantic certificate of an accepted evidence-bearing step is claimed there. Existence is assumed when a theorem uses such a map, rather than asserted for arbitrary FO predicates.

Definition 19 (Token-only witnessability).

A trigger is token-only witnessable if on every satisfying non-social event it has a nonempty validated witness whose restricted predicate instances can be verified from the annotated witness, fixed public context, and any required proof payload, without non-token event metadata. This is a restriction beyond event-relative witnessing in Definition 6. For guarded positive existential triggers, such a certificate also establishes full-event satisfaction; for nonmonotone triggers a separate full-event check remains necessary.

Remark 6.

Extractor existence must be checked for the chosen semantics. A formula requiring an invalid token may be true on the full event but false on every validated-token restriction. Absence conditions can be witnessable yet still require a full-event check. Token-only verification additionally excludes dependence on non-token event metadata.

Certificates and canonicalization.

A (step) certificate is a pair π=(ℓ,W)\pi=(\ell,W) where ℓ∈{1,…,ri}∪{⊥}\ell\in\{1,\dots,r_{i}\}\cup\{\bot\} is a label (a trigger index or the fallback symbol ⊥\bot) and W⊆𝒯W\subseteq\mathcal{T} is the witness set.

Definition 20 (Certificate canonicalization).

Define can⁡(ℓ,W)\mathrm{can}(\ell,W) by

can⁡(ℓ,W):={(⊥,∅),W=∅,(ℓ,W),W≠∅.\mathrm{can}(\ell,W)\;:=\;\begin{cases}(\bot,\emptyset),&W=\emptyset,\\ (\ell,W),&W\neq\emptyset.\end{cases}

Canonicalization records that an empty witness cannot authorize an evidence-bearing transition. It is a projection used for equivalence proofs; the original proposal and rejection reason remain in the operational log.

Certified one-step semantics.

Fix witness extractors Witψi,j\mathrm{Wit}_{\psi_{i,j}} for each trigger ψi,j\psi_{i,j}. Define the certified one-step semantics of PiP_{i} by

F^Pi​(b,E):=(FPi​(b,E),can⁡(πPi​(E))),\widehat{F}_{P_{i}}(b,E)\;:=\;\Big(F_{P_{i}}(b,E),\ \mathrm{can}\big(\pi_{P_{i}}(E)\big)\Big),

where the protocol’s (pre-canonical) certificate map is

πPi​(E):={(jPi⋆​(E),Witψi,jPi⋆​(E)​(E)),JPi​(E)≠∅,(⊥,∅),JPi​(E)=∅.\pi_{P_{i}}(E):=\begin{cases}\big(j^{\star}_{P_{i}}(E),\ \mathrm{Wit}_{\psi_{i,j^{\star}_{P_{i}}(E)}}(E)\big),&J_{P_{i}}(E)\neq\emptyset,\\ (\bot,\emptyset),&J_{P_{i}}(E)=\emptyset.\end{cases}

Similarly, for a PBRC contract CiC_{i} with triggers φi,j\varphi_{i,j} and witness extractors Witφi,j\mathrm{Wit}_{\varphi_{i,j}}, define F^Ci\widehat{F}_{C_{i}} analogously.

Definition 21 (Belief equivalence and audit equivalence).

Two protocols/constraints XX and YY (for the same agent and hypothesis space) are:

  1. 1.

    belief-equivalent, written X≡BYX\equiv_{\mathrm{B}}Y, if FX​(b,E)=FY​(b,E)F_{X}(b,E)=F_{Y}(b,E) for all beliefs bb and events EE (equivalently, they induce identical belief trajectories on every event stream);

  2. 2.

    audit-equivalent, written X≡AYX\equiv_{\mathrm{A}}Y, if F^X​(b,E)=F^Y​(b,E)\widehat{F}_{X}(b,E)=\widehat{F}_{Y}(b,E) for all beliefs bb and events EE (equivalently, they induce identical trajectories of beliefs together with canonicalized certificates on every event stream).

8.3 Evidence-splitting compilation to an evidential PBRC contract

Recall that SocialOnly⁡(E)\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E) means that EE contains no validated token, i.e. 𝒯⁡(E)=∅\mathcal{T}(E)=\emptyset. Equivalently, ¬SocialOnly⁡(E)\neg\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E) holds iff EE contains at least one validated token.

The compilation below separates (i) evidence-present events, where triggers are made explicitly evidence-gated, from (ii) social-only events, where the compiled contract is forced to reproduce the original protocol’s behavior by pushing that behavior into the fallback.22 2 This “evidence-splitting” is intentional. It yields an evidential contract (all triggers require nonempty validated evidence) while preserving the original one-step belief semantics on all events. In later sections, when we impose socially robust constraints (e.g., argmax-preserving fallback on social-only events), the social-only behavior absorbed into the fallback is correspondingly constrained.

Definition 22 (PBRC normal form of a trigger protocol).

Given Pi=⟨(ψi,1,Vi,1),…,(ψi,ri,Vi,ri),≺i,δi⟩P_{i}=\langle(\psi_{i,1},V_{i,1}),\dots,(\psi_{i,r_{i}},V_{i,r_{i}}),\prec_{i},\delta_{i}\rangle, define its PBRC normal form NF⁡(Pi)\mathrm{NF}(P_{i}) as the contract

NF(Pi)=⟨(φi,1,Ui,1),…,(φi,ri,Ui,ri),≺i,δiNF⟩\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})=\langle(\varphi_{i,1},U_{i,1}),\dots,(\varphi_{i,r_{i}},U_{i,r_{i}}),\prec_{i},\delta_{i}^{\mathrm{NF}}\rangle

where for each j∈{1,…,ri}j\in\{1,\dots,r_{i}\},

φi,j:=ψi,j∧¬SocialOnly,Ui,j:=Vi,j,\varphi_{i,j}\;:=\;\psi_{i,j}\ \land\ \neg\mathrm{SocialOnly},\qquad U_{i,j}\;:=\;V_{i,j},

and the fallback δiNF\delta_{i}^{\mathrm{NF}} is defined by

δiNF​(b,E):={FPi​(b,E),SocialOnly⁡(E),δi​(b,E),¬SocialOnly⁡(E).\delta_{i}^{\mathrm{NF}}(b,E):=\begin{cases}F_{P_{i}}(b,E),&\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E),\\ \delta_{i}(b,E),&\neg\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E).\end{cases} (3)
Lemma 3 (Evidentiality of NF⁡(Pi)\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})).

NF⁡(Pi)\mathrm{NF}(P_{i}) is an evidential PBRC contract: for every jj and every event EE,

E⊧φi,j⇒¬SocialOnly⁡(E)⇒∃τ​Valid​(τ).E\models\varphi_{i,j}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\neg\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E)\quad\Rightarrow\quad\exists\tau\ \mathrm{Valid}(\tau).
Proof.

If E⊧φi,jE\models\varphi_{i,j} then by definition of φi,j\varphi_{i,j} we have E⊧¬SocialOnlyE\models\neg\mathrm{SocialOnly}. Unfolding ¬SocialOnly⁡(E)\neg\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E) (equivalently, 𝒯⁡(E)≠∅\mathcal{T}(E)\neq\emptyset) yields that EE contains at least one validated token, i.e. ∃τ​Valid​(τ)\exists\tau\,\mathrm{Valid}(\tau). ∎

8.4 Representation theorem (belief and audit equivalence)

We next show that NF⁡(Pi)\mathrm{NF}(P_{i}) preserves both the induced belief dynamics and the auditor-visible certificate trace (after canonicalization). The only subtlety is the treatment of social-only events: when 𝒯⁡(E)=∅\mathcal{T}(E)=\emptyset, any token-sound witness extractor must return the empty set, so all such “justifications” collapse to fallback under canonicalization.

Lemma 4 (Token-sound witnesses are empty on social-only events).

Let χ\chi be any trigger and let Witχ\mathrm{Wit}_{\chi} satisfy token soundness (Definition 18). If SocialOnly⁡(E)\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E) then Witχ​(E)=∅\mathrm{Wit}_{\chi}(E)=\emptyset.

Proof.

If SocialOnly⁡(E)\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E) then 𝒯⁡(E)=∅\mathcal{T}(E)=\emptyset. Token soundness gives Witχ​(E)⊆𝒯⁡(E)=∅\mathrm{Wit}_{\chi}(E)\subseteq\mathcal{T}(E)=\emptyset, hence Witχ​(E)=∅\mathrm{Wit}_{\chi}(E)=\emptyset. ∎

Theorem 7 (PBRC normal form representation (two equivalences)).

Let PiP_{i} be any auditable trigger protocol and let NF⁡(Pi)\mathrm{NF}(P_{i}) be its PBRC normal form (Definition 22). Then:

  1. 1.

    (belief equivalence) NF(Pi)≡BPi\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})\equiv_{\mathrm{B}}P_{i}; i.e. for all beliefs bb and events EE,

    FNF⁡(Pi)​(b,E)=FPi​(b,E).F_{\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})}(b,E)=F_{P_{i}}(b,E).
  2. 2.

    (audit equivalence) Fix witness extractors Witψi,j\mathrm{Wit}_{\psi_{i,j}} satisfying Definition 18 for the triggers of PiP_{i} and define witness extractors for NF⁡(Pi)\mathrm{NF}(P_{i}) by

    Witφi,j​(E):=Witψi,j​(E)for all ​E,j.\mathrm{Wit}_{\varphi_{i,j}}(E):=\mathrm{Wit}_{\psi_{i,j}}(E)\qquad\text{for all }E,j.

    Then NF(Pi)≡APi\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})\equiv_{\mathrm{A}}P_{i}; i.e. for all b,Eb,E,

    F^NF⁡(Pi)​(b,E)=F^Pi​(b,E).\widehat{F}_{\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})}(b,E)=\widehat{F}_{P_{i}}(b,E).

    Moreover, if ¬SocialOnly⁡(E)\neg\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E) then the uncanonicalized certificates coincide:

    πNF⁡(Pi)​(E)=πPi​(E).\pi_{\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})}(E)=\pi_{P_{i}}(E).

Consequently, for any event stream (Et)t≥0(E^{t})_{t\geq 0} and initial belief b0b^{0}, the two protocols generate identical belief trajectories, and any auditor who canonicalizes empty-witness certificates observes identical certificate traces.

Proof.
(1) Belief equivalence.

Fix bb and EE.

Case 1: SocialOnly⁡(E)\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E). Then ¬SocialOnly⁡(E)\neg\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E) is false, so for every jj the compiled trigger φi,j=ψi,j∧¬SocialOnly\varphi_{i,j}=\psi_{i,j}\land\neg\mathrm{SocialOnly} is false. Hence JNF⁡(Pi)​(E)=∅J_{\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})}(E)=\emptyset and NF⁡(Pi)\mathrm{NF}(P_{i}) applies its fallback:

FNF⁡(Pi)​(b,E)=δiNF​(b,E).F_{\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})}(b,E)=\delta_{i}^{\mathrm{NF}}(b,E).

By (3), δiNF​(b,E)=FPi​(b,E)\delta_{i}^{\mathrm{NF}}(b,E)=F_{P_{i}}(b,E) on social-only events. Thus FNF⁡(Pi)​(b,E)=FPi​(b,E)F_{\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})}(b,E)=F_{P_{i}}(b,E).

Case 2: ¬SocialOnly⁡(E)\neg\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E). Then for each jj we have E⊧φi,jE\models\varphi_{i,j} iff E⊧ψi,jE\models\psi_{i,j}, because the conjunct ¬SocialOnly\neg\mathrm{SocialOnly} holds. Therefore

JNF⁡(Pi)​(E)=JPi​(E),jNF⁡(Pi)⋆​(E)=jPi⋆​(E),J_{\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})}(E)=J_{P_{i}}(E),\qquad j^{\star}_{\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})}(E)=j^{\star}_{P_{i}}(E),

(with the selected-index equality understood only when the common set is nonempty, and using the same priority order ≺i\prec_{i}). If JPi​(E)≠∅J_{P_{i}}(E)\neq\emptyset then both apply the same triggered operator:

FNF⁡(Pi)​(b,E)=Ui,j⋆​(b,E)=Vi,j⋆​(b,E)=FPi​(b,E).F_{\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})}(b,E)=U_{i,j^{\star}}(b,E)=V_{i,j^{\star}}(b,E)=F_{P_{i}}(b,E).

If JPi​(E)=∅J_{P_{i}}(E)=\emptyset, then both take fallback and (3) yields

FNF⁡(Pi)​(b,E)=δiNF​(b,E)=δi​(b,E)=FPi​(b,E).F_{\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})}(b,E)=\delta_{i}^{\mathrm{NF}}(b,E)=\delta_{i}(b,E)=F_{P_{i}}(b,E).

Thus FNF⁡(Pi)​(b,E)=FPi​(b,E)F_{\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})}(b,E)=F_{P_{i}}(b,E) in all cases, proving NF(Pi)≡BPi\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})\equiv_{\mathrm{B}}P_{i}.

(2) Audit equivalence.

On a non-social satisfying event, the original extractor returns a nonempty validated witness that satisfies ψ\psi in its restricted structure. That same restricted structure contains a valid token, so it also satisfies ψ∧¬SocialOnly\psi\land\neg\mathrm{SocialOnly}. Thus the inherited map is a correct extractor for the compiled trigger. Fix bb and EE.

Case 1: SocialOnly⁡(E)\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E). Then 𝒯⁡(E)=∅\mathcal{T}(E)=\emptyset, and by Lemma 4 every token-sound witness extractor returns the empty set: Witψi,j​(E)=∅\mathrm{Wit}_{\psi_{i,j}}(E)=\emptyset for all jj. Hence, regardless of whether PiP_{i} selects a trigger label, its (pre-canonical) certificate has empty witness, so

can⁡(πPi​(E))=(⊥,∅).\mathrm{can}\big(\pi_{P_{i}}(E)\big)=(\bot,\emptyset).

For NF⁡(Pi)\mathrm{NF}(P_{i}), we already established that JNF⁡(Pi)​(E)=∅J_{\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})}(E)=\emptyset, so πNF⁡(Pi)​(E)=(⊥,∅)\pi_{\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})}(E)=(\bot,\emptyset) and therefore can⁡(πNF⁡(Pi)​(E))=(⊥,∅)\mathrm{can}\big(\pi_{\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})}(E)\big)=(\bot,\emptyset). Together with belief equivalence from part (1), this gives

F^NF⁡(Pi)​(b,E)=F^Pi​(b,E).\widehat{F}_{\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})}(b,E)=\widehat{F}_{P_{i}}(b,E).

Case 2: ¬SocialOnly⁡(E)\neg\mathrm{SocialOnly}(E). Then JNF⁡(Pi)​(E)=JPi​(E)J_{\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})}(E)=J_{P_{i}}(E) and hence both protocols select the same trigger label whenever any trigger holds. If JPi​(E)=∅J_{P_{i}}(E)=\emptyset, both certificates are (⊥,∅)(\bot,\emptyset) and canonicalized certificates match. If JPi​(E)≠∅J_{P_{i}}(E)\neq\emptyset, let j⋆=jPi⋆​(E)=jNF⁡(Pi)⋆​(E)j^{\star}=j^{\star}_{P_{i}}(E)=j^{\star}_{\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})}(E). By construction of witness extractors,

Witφi,j⋆​(E)=Witψi,j⋆​(E),\mathrm{Wit}_{\varphi_{i,j^{\star}}}(E)=\mathrm{Wit}_{\psi_{i,j^{\star}}}(E),

so the (pre-canonical) certificates coincide:

πNF⁡(Pi)​(E)=(j⋆,Witφi,j⋆​(E))=(j⋆,Witψi,j⋆​(E))=πPi​(E).\pi_{\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})}(E)=\big(j^{\star},\mathrm{Wit}_{\varphi_{i,j^{\star}}}(E)\big)=\big(j^{\star},\mathrm{Wit}_{\psi_{i,j^{\star}}}(E)\big)=\pi_{P_{i}}(E).

In particular, the canonicalized certificates coincide. Combining with part (1) yields F^NF⁡(Pi)​(b,E)=F^Pi​(b,E)\widehat{F}_{\mathrm{NF}(P_{i})}(b,E)=\widehat{F}_{P_{i}}(b,E).

Trajectories.

Since the one-step belief outputs and canonicalized certificates agree for all (b,E)(b,E), equality of belief trajectories and canonicalized audit traces over any event stream follows by induction on time. ∎

Corollary 2 (Canonical reduction to evidential PBRC without losing auditable evidence-traces).

Within the class of FO-definable auditable trigger protocols equipped with extractors satisfying Definition 18, any update policy is without loss of generality representable as an evidential PBRC contract that is both belief-equivalent and audit-equivalent (Definition 21): all non-fallback updates are explicitly evidence-gated, and the projected certificate trace is preserved.
