10.4 Semantics

A CDDL model is a Kripke structure

M=(W,{Ri}i∈𝒜,{Ra}a∈𝖠𝖼𝗍0,V),M=(W,\{R_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{A}},\{R_{a}\}_{a\in\mathsf{Act}_{0}},V),

where each RiR_{i} is serial, transitive, and Euclidean (KD45 frames), each Ra⊆W×WR_{a}\subseteq W\times W interprets an atomic action, and VV is a valuation. Program relations extend compositionally:

Rα;β\displaystyle R_{\alpha;\beta} :=Rα∘Rβ,Rα∪β:=Rα∪Rβ,Rψ​?:={(w,w):M,w⊧ψ},\displaystyle:=R_{\alpha}\circ R_{\beta},\qquad R_{\alpha\cup\beta}:=R_{\alpha}\cup R_{\beta},\qquad R_{\psi?}:=\{(w,w):M,w\models\psi\},
Rα∗\displaystyle R_{\alpha^{\ast}} :=(Rα)∗(reflexive transitive closure).\displaystyle:=(R_{\alpha})^{\ast}\quad\text{(reflexive transitive closure)}.

Truth is defined by the standard clauses for KD45 belief and PDL:

M,w⊧Biφ⇔∀w′(wRiw′⇒M,w′⊧φ),M,w⊧[α]φ⇔∀w′(wRαw′⇒M,w′⊧φ).M,w\models B_{i}\varphi\iff\forall w^{\prime}\,(wR_{i}w^{\prime}\Rightarrow M,w^{\prime}\models\varphi),\qquad M,w\models[\alpha]\varphi\iff\forall w^{\prime}\,(wR_{\alpha}w^{\prime}\Rightarrow M,w^{\prime}\models\varphi).

10.5 Encoding accepted decisions as programs

Let 𝖭𝗈𝗇𝖾i=¬⋁j𝖠𝖼𝖼i,j\mathsf{None}_{i}=\neg\bigvee_{j}\mathsf{Acc}_{i,j} and define

πi=⋃j=1ki(𝖠𝖼𝖼i,j​?;𝗎𝗉𝖽i,j)∪(𝖭𝗈𝗇𝖾i​?;𝖿𝖻i).\pi_{i}=\bigcup_{j=1}^{k_{i}}(\mathsf{Acc}_{i,j}?;\mathsf{upd}_{i,j})\ \cup\ (\mathsf{None}_{i}?;\mathsf{fb}_{i}).

Write π⁡(Ci)=πi\pi(C_{i})=\pi_{i} when the contract is understood. This encoding covers sound-but-incomplete routers, where a true trigger can still lead to fallback. A program guarded only by raw trigger truth would omit such fallback steps. For a complete router, mutually exclusive priority guards derived from 𝖳𝗋𝗂𝗀i,j\mathsf{Trig}_{i,j} agree with acceptance; this agreement must be checked, not assumed for every router.

Lemma 6 (Run-to-program bridge).

Under Definition 45, Rπi={(t,t+1):0≤t<T}R_{\pi_{i}}=\{(t,t+1):0\leq t<T\}. Hence Rπi∗={(t,u):0≤t≤u≤T}R_{\pi_{i}^{\ast}}=\{(t,u):0\leq t\leq u\leq T\}.

Proof.

Every recorded step has exactly one accepted branch or fallback. Its guard is true and its labeled edge is present, so the step is in RπiR_{\pi_{i}}. Conversely, each branch consists of an identity test followed by one of the recorded edges; no other edge can be introduced. Reflexive transitive closure of the consecutive-index relation yields the second equality. ∎

10.6 PBRC invariants expressed in CDDL

For compactness define the following formula, with hh ranging over the fixed hypothesis set:

𝖲𝗍𝖺𝖻𝗅𝖾i:=⋀h[(𝖳𝗈𝗉i,h→[πi]​𝖳𝗈𝗉i,h)∧(¬𝖳𝗈𝗉i,h→[πi]​¬𝖳𝗈𝗉i,h)].\mathsf{Stable}_{i}:=\bigwedge_{h}\left[(\mathsf{Top}_{i,h}\to[\pi_{i}]\mathsf{Top}_{i,h})\land(\neg\mathsf{Top}_{i,h}\to[\pi_{i}]\neg\mathsf{Top}_{i,h})\right].

Both implications are necessary: preserving existing maximizers alone permits new ties. Social-only equality of the entire top set is expressed by

[πi∗]​(𝖲𝗈𝖼𝖮𝗇𝗅𝗒i→𝖲𝗍𝖺𝖻𝗅𝖾i).[\pi_{i}^{\ast}](\mathsf{SocOnly}_{i}\to\mathsf{Stable}_{i}). (4)

With argmax-preserving fallback, accountability can be expressed at the source state as

[πi∗]​(¬𝖠𝖼𝖼i→𝖲𝗍𝖺𝖻𝗅𝖾i).[\pi_{i}^{\ast}](\neg\mathsf{Acc}_{i}\to\mathsf{Stable}_{i}). (5)

Equivalently, any change in the complete top set requires an accepted non-fallback decision at that step’s source. Sound routing must separately establish that the decision has a valid nonempty witness for the full-event selected trigger. Testing a trigger atom after the step would instead inspect the next event and would not certify the transition under review.

These formulas hold under the corresponding operational assumptions by the bridge lemma and the fallback theorems. On a terminal logged state, boxes for one-step actions are vacuously true. A completed finite-prefix check certifies only recorded transitions; it does not establish what happens after the log ends.

10.7 Axioms and proof rules

We use a standard Hilbert system consisting of:

  • •

    propositional tautologies and modus ponens;

  • •

    KD45 axioms for each BiB_{i} (normality 𝐊\mathbf{K}, seriality 𝐃\mathbf{D}, positive introspection 𝟒\mathbf{4}, negative introspection 𝟓\mathbf{5}) and necessitation for BiB_{i};

  • •

    normality for dynamic modalities and necessitation for [α][\alpha];

  • •

    PDL reduction axioms:

    𝐒𝐞𝐪:\displaystyle\mathbf{Seq}: [α;β]​φ↔[α]​[β]​φ,\displaystyle\ [\alpha;\beta]\varphi\leftrightarrow[\alpha][\beta]\varphi,
    𝐂𝐡𝐨𝐢𝐜𝐞:\displaystyle\mathbf{Choice}: [α∪β]​φ↔([α]​φ∧[β]​φ),\displaystyle\ [\alpha\cup\beta]\varphi\leftrightarrow([\alpha]\varphi\land[\beta]\varphi),
    𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭:\displaystyle\mathbf{Test}: [ψ​?]​φ↔(ψ→φ);\displaystyle\ [\psi?]\varphi\leftrightarrow(\psi\to\varphi);
  • •

    the star axiom and induction rule:

    𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐫:\displaystyle\mathbf{Star}: [α∗]​φ↔(φ∧[α]​[α∗]​φ),\displaystyle\ [\alpha^{\ast}]\varphi\leftrightarrow\big(\varphi\land[\alpha][\alpha^{\ast}]\varphi\big),
    𝐈𝐧𝐝:\displaystyle\mathbf{Ind}: from ​(φ→[α]​φ)​ infer ​(φ→[α∗]​φ).\displaystyle\ \text{from }(\varphi\to[\alpha]\varphi)\ \text{ infer }(\varphi\to[\alpha^{\ast}]\varphi).

Necessitation and 𝐈𝐧𝐝\mathbf{Ind} apply to theorems (globally valid premises), not to a premise assumed only at one state. No interaction axioms between numerical beliefs, BiB_{i}, and action relations are postulated.

10.8 Soundness and finite-model checking

Theorem 23 (Soundness of CDDL).

Every theorem of the stated proof system is valid in every model with serial, transitive, Euclidean doxastic relations and the specified PDL program semantics, including reflexive transitive closure for iteration.

Proof.

Each axiom is valid and each rule preserves global validity; Appendix A proves these statements and induction on derivations yields the conclusion. ∎

Theorem 24 (Exact finite-model monitoring).

Given an explicit finite model, formula valuations and program relations can be computed exactly by mutual structural recursion, with finite relational closure for star. In particular, the BiB_{i}-free formulas above are decidable on any finite instrumented run. Including BiB_{i} is possible when its accessibility relations are supplied.

Proof.

See Appendix A for the algorithm and its structural correctness proof. This result concerns a given finite model, not completeness of the Hilbert system over all models. ∎

Audit procedure.

First validate log integrity, full-event annotations, priority selection, certificates, and numerical updates using stored inputs and versioned validators. Next construct the run graph and check that every recorded step has exactly one correctly labeled edge. Evaluate the source atoms, then the formulas. For a failed invariant, report its earliest violating source index and actual successor together with the rejected check. A violated assumption can be located in the log; determining whether a token’s semantic assertion is true may still require external evidence.

11 Design and implementation guidelines

PBRC is intentionally protocol-level: it specifies which public artifacts (contracts, tokens, certificates, and audit traces) must exist for belief change to be admissible and verifiable, while remaining agnostic to how agents generate messages. The goal is to preserve open communication while making changes of mind evidence-gated, auditable, and (under a state-holding router) enforceable.

This section distills implementation guidance that preserves the paper’s formal guarantees in deployed multi-agent systems. The recurring theme is to (i) keep triggers witnessable by small token sets, (ii) separate cryptographic validity from semantic applicability, and (iii) choose conservative operators and fallbacks that make safety robust to missing or delayed evidence.

11.1 Contract patterns (templates)

In practice, many contracts can be assembled from a small library of reusable patterns. For predictability and efficiency, these are best restricted to token-witnessable fragments such as FO∃⁣∧𝖳𝗈𝗄\mathrm{FO}^{\mathsf{Tok}}_{\exists\wedge} (Definition 46), where admissibility can be certified by a small witness set and checked locally (Propositions 8–9).

Verified contradiction (falsifier pattern). A conservative default is to permit decreases in belief mass (or argmax flips away from a hypothesis) only when a validated token contradicts that hypothesis, e.g.,

∃τ⁡(Valid⁡(τ)∧Contradicts⁡(τ,h)).\exists\tau\;\big(\mathrm{Valid}(\tau)\wedge\mathrm{Contradicts}(\tau,h)\big).

Operationally, contradiction triggers are the primary safeguard against “wrong-but-sure” cascades driven by social pressure: if no validated contradictor exists, social exchange cannot justify moving probability mass aggressively.

Verified support (bounded confirmation). When positive evidence is available, include support triggers of the form

∃τ⁡(Valid⁡(τ)∧Supports⁡(τ,h)),\exists\tau\;\big(\mathrm{Valid}(\tau)\wedge\mathrm{Supports}(\tau,h)\big),

but couple them with bounded operators (e.g., capped log-odds steps or margin-based updates) to avoid runaway overconfidence from a single token or noisy verifier. In many settings, it is appropriate to require stronger conditions for increasing confidence than for decreasing it (e.g., support requires kk independent attestations; contradiction requires one strong falsifier).

Freshness gating (replay resistance). To control replay and context drift, augment evidence triggers with freshness predicates:

∃τ⁡(Valid⁡(τ)∧Supports⁡(τ,h)∧FreshΔ​(τ,t)),\exists\tau\;\big(\mathrm{Valid}(\tau)\wedge\mathrm{Supports}(\tau,h)\wedge\mathrm{Fresh}_{\Delta}(\tau,t)\big),

and analogously for contradiction. This implements the theoretical replay bounds (Theorem 20) and is typically cheap in the logical layer (constant-time arithmetic checks per token).

Multi-attestation (robustness to validator compromise). When the validity layer admits attestations, replace single-token conditions by quorum-like requirements (“kk-of-KK”) at the validity layer (Section 9). This reduces the impact of any single compromised validator or verifier and yields an explicit robustness–liveness trade-off: larger kk improves integrity but may delay admissible revision when evidence is sparse.

Surprise clauses (novel or unmodeled evidence). Because preregistration can be brittle, include a low-priority clause that activates when a validated token is present but does not match existing templates, e.g.,

∃τ⁡(Valid⁡(τ)∧Unmodeled⁡(τ)).\exists\tau\;\big(\mathrm{Valid}(\tau)\wedge\mathrm{Unmodeled}(\tau)\big).

Within the fixed-state model the corresponding operator should conservatively hold or dilute belief. Deferral actions, tool calls, and hypothesis expansion require extensions to the state and action semantics (Section 3.2). Importantly, surprise clauses do not weaken the anti-conformity story: in the token-empty regime they never fire, and social-only exchange remains routed to fallback.

Budget clauses (availability and DoS resilience). A practical attack surface is flooding events with many tokens (valid but irrelevant) to inflate validation latency. Two complementary mitigations are recommended: (i) use positive witnessable triggers so checking can stop once the highest-priority branch is established; lower-priority branches also require ruling out all higher-priority triggers (Section 13.7); and (ii) enforce explicit per-round validation budgets with a safe defer/hold fallback when budgets are exceeded. Budget predicates are naturally router-side (policy-level) and can be treated as part of the enforcement environment rather than the agent’s private computation.

11.2 Token validity and semantic applicability

A common deployment failure is to conflate cryptographic validity with semantic applicability. In PBRC, the validity layer is the boundary at which evidence becomes admissible; if this boundary is underspecified, the system becomes vulnerable to “citation laundering” (valid provenance, irrelevant content) or to entailment mislabeling (valid tokens, incorrect Supports/Contradicts mapping).

A robust token schema should therefore bind evidence to task context and support auditing. Concretely, tokens should (at minimum) include: (i) a provenance binding (signatures/attestations), (ii) a timestamp (for freshness checks), (iii) a context binding (instance identifier, prompt hash, or task context hash), and (iv) typed content (tool output schema, retrieval snippet hash, verifier judgment metadata). At the predicate level, the router should be able to expose at least:

Valid⁡(τ),FreshΔ​(τ,t),Type⁡(τ,⋅),\mathrm{Valid}(\tau),\quad\mathrm{Fresh}_{\Delta}(\tau,t),\quad\mathrm{Type}(\tau,\cdot),

and, when feasible, a separate predicate capturing applicability (e.g., “the snippet is about the claim”), distinct from semantic entailment. When entailment-based labeling is used, auditability improves substantially if tokens record the verifier identity/version and the exact inputs used to compute the label (so that the Supports/Contradicts relation is reproducible).

Finally, because social influence can act indirectly by steering evidence generation (biased queries, selective tool calls), the validity layer should, where possible, bind tokens to the inputs that generated them (query hashes, tool-call arguments). This supports query-policy compliance mechanisms (Section 9.2) and helps prevent conformity-by-proxy.

11.3 Worked contract: peer-pressure misinformation triage

We describe a proposed contract for a binary misinformation triage task in which peer interaction may be persuasive but unreliable.

Hypotheses. Let ℋ={real,fake}\mathcal{H}=\{\textsf{real},\textsf{fake}\} denote the claim status.

Token families and validity layer. We use two token families: (1) tool tokens τtool\tau_{\mathrm{tool}} representing signed outputs of a fact-checking tool/API (structured verdict + provenance), and (2) retrieval tokens τret\tau_{\mathrm{ret}} binding a snippet hash, URL, and timestamp to a retrieval procedure. The validity layer verifies provenance, checks freshness, binds tokens to the instance context, and exposes Supports⁡(⋅,⋅)\mathrm{Supports}(\cdot,\cdot) / Contradicts⁡(⋅,⋅)\mathrm{Contradicts}(\cdot,\cdot) predicates (e.g., via a pinned verifier model with logged inputs/outputs).

Triggers and priority. A conservative contract prioritizes high-integrity tool evidence over weaker retrieval evidence. One example trigger set is:

φtool​_​con\displaystyle\varphi_{\mathrm{tool\_con}} :=∃τ⁡(App⁡(τ,t)∧Type⁡(τ,tool)∧Contradicts⁡(τ,real)),\displaystyle:=\exists\tau\;(\mathrm{App}(\tau,t)\wedge\mathrm{Type}(\tau,\mathrm{tool})\wedge\mathrm{Contradicts}(\tau,\textsf{real})),
φtool​_​sup\displaystyle\varphi_{\mathrm{tool\_sup}} :=∃τ⁡(App⁡(τ,t)∧Type⁡(τ,tool)∧Supports⁡(τ,real)),\displaystyle:=\exists\tau\;(\mathrm{App}(\tau,t)\wedge\mathrm{Type}(\tau,\mathrm{tool})\wedge\mathrm{Supports}(\tau,\textsf{real})),
φret​_​con\displaystyle\varphi_{\mathrm{ret\_con}} :=∃τ⁡(App⁡(τ,t)∧Type⁡(τ,ret)∧Contradicts⁡(τ,real)∧FreshΔ​(τ,t)).\displaystyle:=\exists\tau\;(\mathrm{App}(\tau,t)\wedge\mathrm{Type}(\tau,\mathrm{ret})\wedge\mathrm{Contradicts}(\tau,\textsf{real})\wedge\mathrm{Fresh}_{\Delta}(\tau,t)).

A typical priority policy checks tool-based triggers first and treats retrieval-based contradiction as weaker, freshness-gated evidence. (Equivalently, the priority order φtool​_​con≺φtool​_​sup≺φret​_​con\varphi_{\mathrm{tool\_con}}\prec\varphi_{\mathrm{tool\_sup}}\prec\varphi_{\mathrm{ret\_con}} is chosen so that tool triggers dominate retrieval triggers under the contract’s selection rule.)

Operators and fallback. Operators should be bounded and auditable (e.g., capped log-odds steps). For example, φtool​_​con\varphi_{\mathrm{tool\_con}} applies a strong bounded decrease to b⁡(real)b(\textsf{real}), φtool​_​sup\varphi_{\mathrm{tool\_sup}} applies a bounded increase, and φret​_​con\varphi_{\mathrm{ret\_con}} applies a smaller bounded decrease. In trigger-inactive rounds (including social-only exchange), the enforced update is fallback; an argmax-preserving skeptical dilution δλ\delta_{\lambda} is a safe default when the objective is to prevent confidence escalation under persuasion.

Certificates and post-hoc audit. Any top-hypothesis change is accompanied by a nonempty witness set (Theorem 17) identifying the validated token(s) that licensed the change. If the system later exhibits a first incorrect flip, the failure localization theorem (Theorem 22) narrows the diagnosis to evidence integrity failures (forgery/compromise), contextual validity failures (replay/staleness), router unsoundness, or contract/operator misspecification, with numerical operator noncompliance included as a separate possible failure.

11.4 Supplementary finite token-set implementation

We implement a state-holding reference router for finite token-set predicates. It selects the highest-priority true predicate on the full validated set, requires a nonempty valid witness satisfying the selected predicate on restriction, executes the registered operator, and checks the numerical output before committing state. The default witness is the full validated set; this is sound for the implemented token-set semantics but does not promise a small certificate. Custom extractors are checked independently. An incomplete decision rejects the selected branch and uses fallback; it does not discard tokens and then accept a lower-priority branch. Coverage is reported as unobserved if the supplied horizon ends before closure.

The validator and its version identifier are mandatory, and tokens with conflicting contents under one identifier are rejected. Logs retain full events, validation decisions, proposed and executed certificates, failures, and before/after beliefs. Deterministic replay additionally requires immutable callback code, parameters, and context. The 27 regression tests cover witness sufficiency, full-event truth, priority, validation, contextual freshness, numerical failures, state integrity, random-state separation, and knowledge/exposure distinctions. An invalid fallback raises without committing a numerical state.

The implementation assumes well-typed input objects and trusted local callbacks; it implements neither signatures nor arbitrary first-order satisfaction, and its logs are not tamper-evident. The probability-vector check permits a 10−1210^{-12} rounding tolerance in normalization. Thus these finite checks support the implementation within its stated scope, not a floating-point proof of the real-arithmetic theorems or a production-security claim.

11.5 Contract verification and synthesis

Contracts can be verified against global safety invariants expressed in CDDL (Section 10) and audited post hoc using full inputs, decisions, certificates, and numerical state transitions (Proposition 6). A finite log check establishes only that recorded execution; a global guarantee requires a proof or an explicit transition model covering all allowed executions. Beyond manual design, an important research direction is contract synthesis: propose candidate trigger/operator sets from logs and desired invariants (e.g., “no top-hypothesis flips without evidence”), then validate candidates by model checking against the contract logic and by empirical stress tests under verifier noise, incomplete routers, and adversarial token floods. Even in the absence of fully automated synthesis, the template library above provides a practical starting point for systematic contract engineering.

12 Verification complexity and cost model

12.1 Separate costs and complete checks

Let n=|𝒯⁡(E)|n=|\mathcal{T}(E)|, let kk count quantified token variables, and let LL denote formula encoding size. The cost of reading the event and authenticating its tokens is separate from logical checking. A complete accepted decision must establish event membership and validity of witness tokens, restricted witness satisfaction, full-event trigger truth, priority selection, and correct numerical execution. A schematic accounting is

Cstep=Cparse+Cvalidate+Cwitness+Cfull/priority+Cupdate+Clog.C_{\rm step}=C_{\rm parse}+C_{\rm validate}+C_{\rm witness}+C_{\rm full/priority}+C_{\rm update}+C_{\rm log}.

For monotone positive triggers a supplied witness can establish full-event truth. It does not by itself show that all higher-priority triggers are false. With nonmonotone formulas, even full-event truth of the named trigger needs an additional check. Signature checking and semantic labeling costs depend on the chosen implementation; they are not constant by assumption here.

12.2 A guarded existential conjunctive fragment

Definition 46 (Guarded token-existential conjunctive triggers).

A trigger in FO∃⁣∧𝖳𝗈𝗄\mathrm{FO}^{\mathsf{Tok}}_{\exists\wedge} has the form

χ=∃τ1⋯∃τk(⋀r=1kValid(τr)∧⋀m=1MRm(τ¯m,c¯m)),k≥1.\chi=\exists\tau_{1}\cdots\exists\tau_{k}\left(\bigwedge_{r=1}^{k}\mathrm{Valid}(\tau_{r})\land\bigwedge_{m=1}^{M}R_{m}(\bar{\tau}_{m},\bar{c}_{m})\right),\qquad k\geq 1.

The RmR_{m} are positive atomic predicates, with equality and disequality permitted, over token variables and fixed public parameters. Their interpretations are fixed under token restriction and do not encode aggregates that change when other tokens are added. Each quantified variable is validity-guarded. Token-only use additionally requires that all predicates and parameters agree across the compared events.

Freshness is permitted when time and context are fixed for the comparison; changing either invalidates that comparison. A threshold over authenticated distinct validator identities is not equivalent to counting arbitrary token objects.

Proposition 8 (Assignment certificates and bounded witnesses).

If E⊧χE\models\chi, a satisfying assignment σ=(τ1,…,τk)\sigma=(\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{k}) has image W⊆𝒯⁡(E)W\subseteq\mathcal{T}(E) with 1≤|W|≤k1\leq|W|\leq k, and WW witnesses χ\chi. Given σ\sigma, its validity and conjuncts can be checked in O⁡(k+L)O(k+L) time after constant-time indexed predicate and membership access, excluding token authentication costs. For bounded arity and MM conjuncts this is O⁡(k+M)O(k+M).

Proof.

Validity guards place each assigned value in 𝒯⁡(E)\mathcal{T}(E); k≥1k\geq 1 makes its image nonempty. Restriction to that image preserves all assigned atomic facts and fixed parameters, so the same assignment satisfies the restricted formula. Reading the assignment and checking every conjunct once gives the stated cost. ∎

A witness set alone need not identify which token fills which variable. Reconstructing an assignment may require search; enumerating nkn^{k} tuples gives a simple O​(nk​(k+L))O(n^{k}(k+L)) bound. Thus inexpensive verification of a supplied assignment must not be confused with uniformly efficient witness search when kk is part of the input.

Proposition 9 (Canonical assignment witnesses).

Fix a public total order on token identifiers. On a satisfying finite event, choose the lexicographically least satisfying kk-tuple and return its image and assignment payload. On an unsatisfying event return the empty result. This defines a sound nonvacuous witness extractor; it is token-invariant when the underlying predicates and parameters are token-invariant.

Proof.

There are finitely many tuples, so a nonempty set of satisfying tuples has a unique least member. Proposition 8 proves witness correctness and nonemptiness. Equal annotated token inputs yield the same satisfying tuples, public order, least tuple, and image. Social-only inputs have no tuple satisfying the validity guards. ∎

Canonical selection can require more work than finding any witness. The existence theorem does not assert an efficient canonicalization algorithm for variable-size queries.

12.3 General first-order triggers and caching

A fixed first-order query on a finite explicitly represented structure can be evaluated by recursively enumerating quantified variables, in polynomial data complexity with an exponent depending on the query. This does not give a uniform polynomial bound in query size or guarantee small token witnesses for unrestricted formulas. Full-event negation, universal conditions, and priority checks may require examining data outside an accepted witness.

Under the full assumptions of token-trace equivalence, replay can use complete annotated token exposures, the initial belief, contracts, deterministic operator semantics, and router decisions (or deterministic complete selection). Proposition 6 explains why accepted witnesses alone are insufficient. Cache keys must include the relevant context, current time, validator/schema version, and revocation state. Authentication of immutable contents may be reusable while freshness and applicability still require reevaluation.

Budget exhaustion should cause a logged fallback or deferral decision. Early stopping is justified for a positive highest-priority trigger after a sufficient assignment is found; accepting a lower-priority trigger additionally requires certifying the absence of a higher-priority match. Arbitrary first-order contracts do not inherit the short-circuit cost of the simple toy experiment.

13 Experimental evaluation

We evaluate PBRC through controlled simulations, a matched synthetic study of label errors, a token-empty KAIROS analysis, and an evidence-enabled SciFact experiment. These settings examine different aspects of protocol behavior: social amplification, evidence propagation, validator error, and answer admission. Results are analyzed separately because the tasks, models, and observables differ.

13.1 Metrics and reproducibility

Confidence is conf⁡(b)=maxh⁡b⁡(h)\mathrm{conf}(b)=\max_{h}b(h); accuracy and harmful/beneficial flips require ground truth. Cascade rates use the specific final-state definition below. Cost results count token checks, not wall-clock latency or cryptographic operations. Wilson 95% intervals accompany the cascade proportions in Table 3.

The simulation code builds on https://github.com/alqithami/PBRC, commit 37bbe372b75d5acb8c2df68087900161ca260566. The accompanying source package contains the executable implementations, configurations, raw results, and figure-generation inputs used here. The simulation environment is Python 3.12.14, NumPy 2.3.5, pandas 2.2.3, NetworkX 3.7, and SciPy 1.17.0. Simulations I–V use seed 0; the matched study specifies its seed and repeated-trial design below.

The simulation validator is a trusted callback, and the simulation router computes transitions from caller-supplied state. The reference implementation in Section 11.4 additionally holds and validates its own numerical state. Both implementations have finite token-set semantics; production authentication, semantic validation, and arbitrary first-order enforcement require additional components.

13.2 Simulation I: social-only wrong-but-sure cascades are eliminated by PBRC

This experiment targets the primary failure mode PBRC is designed to prevent: token-empty deliberation (no externally validated evidence) producing a confident but incorrect group outcome via social reinforcement.

Setup. We consider n=20n=20 agents and a binary hypothesis space ℋ={h0,h1}\mathcal{H}=\{h_{0},h_{1}\} with ground truth h0h_{0}. Each agent maintains an explicit belief bit∈Δ⁡(ℋ)b_{i}^{t}\in\Delta(\mathcal{H}). Initial beliefs are drawn i.i.d. as bi0​(h0)∼Beta⁡(5,5)b_{i}^{0}(h_{0})\sim\mathrm{Beta}(5,5), placing agents near the competence boundary so that either hypothesis can dominate early aggregates. We compare two dynamics over T=10T=10 rounds:

  1. 1.

    Baseline (social pooling + confidence amplification). On a graph GG, agent ii forms a neighbor aggregate sits_{i}^{t} and updates by a degree-modulated geometric mixture followed by sharpening:

    bit+1∝(bit)1−wi⋅(sit)wi,bit+1←Sharpenγ​(bit+1),b_{i}^{t+1}\;\propto\;\big(b_{i}^{t}\big)^{1-w_{i}}\cdot\big(s_{i}^{t}\big)^{w_{i}},\qquad b_{i}^{t+1}\leftarrow\mathrm{Sharpen}_{\gamma}(b_{i}^{t+1}),

    where sit=1|N⁡(i)∪{i}|​∑j∈N⁡(i)∪{i}bjts_{i}^{t}=\frac{1}{|N(i)\cup\{i\}|}\sum_{j\in N(i)\cup\{i\}}b_{j}^{t} is the arithmetic mean of neighbor beliefs, wi=min⁡{0.95,w0+ws⋅deg⁡(i)/(n−1)}w_{i}=\min\{0.95,\,w_{0}+w_{s}\cdot\deg(i)/(n-1)\} controls susceptibility to neighbors, and

    Sharpenγ​(p)​(h):=p​(h)γ∑h′∈ℋp​(h′)γ\mathrm{Sharpen}_{\gamma}(p)(h):=\frac{p(h)^{\gamma}}{\sum_{h^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H}}p(h^{\prime})^{\gamma}}

    models confidence amplification.

  2. 2.

    PBRC (evidential contract in token-empty rounds). No validated tokens are present (all events are SocialOnly). Routers reject empty-witness certificates, hence no trigger fires and the enforced update is fallback. We use the argmax-preserving skeptical-dilution fallback bit+1=(1−λ)​bit+λ⋅Unifb_{i}^{t+1}=(1-\lambda)b_{i}^{t}+\lambda\cdot\mathrm{Unif}, which satisfies the social-only non-amplification conditions in Theorem 2.

Unless otherwise stated, (w0,ws,γ,λ)=(0.4,0.5,2.0,0.1)(w_{0},w_{s},\gamma,\lambda)=(0.4,0.5,2.0,0.1).

Representative run. Figure 7 shows a representative complete-graph trajectory in which a minority of agents begins confidently wrong. The baseline dynamics amplify confidence and can pull the population toward the confident minority, illustrating a wrong-but-sure cascade mechanism driven purely by social reinforcement. This illustration uses a different initialization from the cascade-rate trials: 75% of agents have true-hypothesis probabilities uniform on [0.55,0.65][0.55,0.65], and 25% have probabilities uniform on [0.01,0.05][0.01,0.05]. PBRC preserves each initial top hypothesis while diluting confidence; it does not correct initially wrong agents.

Cascade rate versus topology. We operationalize a wrong-but-sure cascade as the event that all agents end with argmax​biT≠h0\mathrm{argmax}b_{i}^{T}\neq h_{0} and conf⁡(biT)≥0.9\mathrm{conf}(b_{i}^{T})\geq 0.9. Across 500500 trials per topology, the baseline exhibits substantial cascade rates on denser graphs, while PBRC eliminates these purely social cascades (Table 3 and Figure 8). The baseline explicitly includes confidence sharpening, so this comparison illustrates that chosen mechanism rather than establishing superiority over arbitrary social-learning policies. The symmetric Beta⁡(5,5)\mathrm{Beta}(5,5) initialization gives each agent a 50% probability of initially favoring the true hypothesis. PBRC preserves those initial choices; its zero observed cascade rate is not an accuracy gain. The theory rules out newly created cascades under its initial-confidence conditions, not already incorrect confident states.

13.3 Simulation I(b): dilution ablation

Theorem 2 is qualitative: in token-empty rounds, if enforcement reduces updates to fallback and the fallback is non-amplifying (and argmax-preserving for top-hypothesis stability), purely social exchange cannot generate wrong-but-sure cascades. Nevertheless, the fallback choice controls confidence decay. This token-empty experiment does not measure evidence-based correction or liveness.

Setup and results. We ablate the skeptical-dilution parameter λ∈{0,0.02,0.05,0.1,0.2,0.4}\lambda\in\{0,0.02,0.05,0.1,0.2,0.4\}. Figure 9 summarizes the outcome. Across topologies, PBRC’s wrong-but-sure cascade rate remains 00 throughout this ablation, while the baseline exhibits nontrivial cascade rates. At the same time, increasing λ\lambda decreases mean confidence at TT by driving beliefs toward uniform more aggressively. This supports the design guidance in Section 11: λ\lambda is best treated as an explicit governance parameter that regulates how strongly the system de-amplifies unvalidated social influence, rather than as a correctness-critical constant.

13.4 Simulation II: token-sufficiency / persuasion separation

This experiment empirically instantiates Theorem 10 in a minimal, fully enforceable setting.

Setup. We fix a token-invariant PBRC contract with two evidential triggers: “∃\exists validated token supporting h0h_{0}” and “∃\exists validated token supporting h1h_{1}”. The router holds the belief state and computes the contract operator (matching the enforceability boundary assumed in Section 4.4). We generate 20002000 pairs of events (E,E′)(E,E^{\prime}) that are token-equivalent (same validated token set) but differ arbitrarily in rhetorical content (sender identity, message text, and confidence fields).

Result. Across all trials, the enforced updates match exactly (observed mismatch rate 00), consistent with the theorem for the implemented token-only operators. This checks a construction that ignores the altered metadata; it is not a test of an LLM’s susceptibility to rhetoric.

13.5 Simulation III: topology affects PBRC only via token arrival times

This experiment validates the topological characterization of evidence closure under flooding dissemination.

Setup and result. We place a unique token at each node and simulate flooding under several connected graph families (ring, ER, star, complete, grid). For each graph, we measure the time until every agent possesses every token, counting its own initial token at time zero. Consistent with Corollary 6, the observed closure time equals the graph diameter in all tested instances (Figure 10). This checks accumulated knowledge closure. Incoming per-round exposures instead use the positive-walk formula of Theorem 12; initial possession is not an incoming message.

13.6 Simulation IV: sound-but-incomplete routers preserve safety but reduce liveness

Many results in Sections 6–8 assume routers that are sound and complete with respect to token validation. Operationally, incompleteness (false negatives) is common due to timeouts, conservative parsing, or strict rate limits.

Setup. We simulate a single-agent setting with a persistent valid evidence token supporting the true hypothesis. The router is sound but incomplete: with probability qq it fails to recognize the token in a given round (false negative), and thus rejects the evidential trigger even though it is semantically satisfied.

Result. For each q∈{0,0.1,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8}q\in\{0,0.1,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8\} the code runs 2,000 trials with a 30-round horizon. It records 31 for trials without correction. Thus Figure 11 reports the mean of min⁡(H,31)\min(H,31), where HH is the first successful round, rather than an uncensored hitting-time estimate. Under independent per-round misses, 𝔼⁡[min⁡(H,31)]=(1−q31)/(1−q)\mathbb{E}[\min(H,31)]=(1-q^{31})/(1-q); the infinite-horizon mean is 1/(1−q)1/(1-q). Larger qq delays correction in this one-token setting. Consistent with Proposition 1, safety remains intact—no belief flip occurs without a validated witness—while liveness degrades as evidence recognition becomes less reliable.

13.7 Simulation V: token flooding and verification cost

PBRC’s enforceability rests on token validation and trigger checking, which exposes an availability surface: flooding events with many tokens (possibly valid but irrelevant) increases verification latency and can induce denial-of-service behavior if not budgeted.

Setup. We model an event containing NN tokens of which exactly one is relevant to the highest-priority trigger. We compare (i) full validation (validate all NN tokens) and (ii) short-circuit validation (validate tokens until a sufficient witness for the highest-priority trigger is found). Under random ordering, the expected number of checks for short-circuiting is exactly (N+1)/2(N{+}1)/2, whereas adversarial ordering negates this benefit.

Result and implications. Figure 12 plots this abstract check-count model, using 2,000 sampled relevant-token positions per N∈{1,6,…,496}N\in\{1,6,\ldots,496\}. It does not measure cryptographic validation, semantic inference, wall-clock latency, or general first-order priority checks. The experiment motivates two complementary mitigation patterns developed in Section 12: (a) adopt token-witnessable trigger fragments with small witnesses (enabling early stopping), and (b) enforce per-round validation budgets with explicit deferral fallbacks when budgets are exceeded.

13.8 Matched evidence study under label errors

This experiment examines how admission thresholds interact with independent and correlated token-label errors. It compares PBRC with an evidence-only updater using the same numerical operator, a social-pooling comparator, and no interaction. The configuration was fixed locally before execution; code, configurations, and trial-level trajectories accompany the results.

Matched trial design.

With seed 20260923, we generate 400 independent trials. Each has 25 agents on an undirected Erdős–Rényi graph with edge probability 0.150.15, conditioned on connectivity by rejection sampling. Ground truth y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\} is a fair draw; each initial probability of the truth is independently Beta⁡(4,6)\mathrm{Beta}(4,6), deliberately favoring an initially incorrect prediction on average. Five distinct token holders are sampled without replacement. Their five tokens have distinct issuer identities and underlying claims equal to yy. A synthetic allow-list validates exact token objects, without implementing cryptography or semantic entailment.

We flip each token’s support label with probability ϵ∈{0,0.1,…,0.5}\epsilon\in\{0,0.1,\ldots,0.5\}. In the independent regime the five flips are independent; in the fully correlated regime one common flip determines all five labels. Labels remain fixed throughout a trial. Graphs, priors, holders, and error uniforms are shared across compared methods; the same uniforms couple the error-rate settings. These are 12 repeated conditions on 400 independent trial inputs, not 4,800 independent task draws. Eight synchronous rounds forward all retained tokens to neighbors and to the sender itself. With these explicit self-loops, incoming exposure after a delivery equals the newly retained knowledge set. Full coverage occurs by round 8 in 399 trials; the remaining trial is retained without imputation.

Operators and comparators.

Let pit=bit​(h1)p_{i}^{t}=b_{i}^{t}(h_{1}), ℓi0=logit⁡(pi0)\ell_{i}^{0}=\operatorname{logit}(p_{i}^{0}), and let ci,htc_{i,h}^{t} count distinct exposed tokens labelled hh after tt deliveries. The evidence-only updater recomputes

pi,evt=σ⁡(ℓi0+log⁡(4)​(ci,1t−ci,0t)),σ⁡(x)=11+e−x.p_{i,\mathrm{ev}}^{t}=\sigma\!\left(\ell_{i}^{0}+\log(4)(c_{i,1}^{t}-c_{i,0}^{t})\right),\qquad\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}.

The fixed weight log⁡(4)\log(4) is an experimental parameter, not an estimated likelihood ratio for each noise level. PBRC uses the same anchored operator when some label has at least kk tokens and strictly more tokens than the other label, for k∈{1,3,5}k\in\{1,3,5\}. Otherwise it applies δ0.1\delta_{0.1}. Priority is h1h_{1} before h0h_{0}; the strict-majority branches cannot both hold. The full exposed set is the witness, and full-event truth is checked because majority can change when tokens are added. Recomputing from the fixed initial anchor deduplicates repeated evidence and makes an unchanged accepted set numerically idempotent; it does not require a newly acquired token at every accepted step.

No interaction holds the initial belief fixed. A specified social comparator averages current neighbor logits, excluding self, mixes this with the current local logit at weight 1/21/2, sharpens by a factor of 2, and then adds log⁡(4)\log(4) times the net count of newly encountered tokens. Writing ℓ¯it−1\bar{\ell}_{i}^{t-1} for the neighbor mean and Δ​ci,ht\Delta c_{i,h}^{t} for new distinct-token counts, its update is

pi,soct=σ⁡(clip[−20,20]⁡[ℓit−1+ℓ¯it−1+log⁡(4)​(Δ​ci,1t−Δ​ci,0t)]).p_{i,\mathrm{soc}}^{t}=\sigma\!\left(\operatorname{clip}_{[-20,20]}\left[\ell_{i}^{t-1}+\bar{\ell}_{i}^{t-1}+\log(4)(\Delta c_{i,1}^{t}-\Delta c_{i,0}^{t})\right]\right).

The comparator’s seen-token set is initially empty, so locally held tokens count on its first round. It has the same evidence budget but different dynamics; it is one specified pooling baseline, not a tuned or universally representative competitor. All parameters were fixed before inspecting outcomes.

Measurement and verification.

Prediction selects h1h_{1} when pit≥1/2p_{i}^{t}\geq 1/2. Metrics first average over agents within a trial. The binary Brier score is (1−bit​(y))2(1-b_{i}^{t}(y))^{2}, rather than the two-class sum; lower is better, but this score alone does not establish calibration. Final harmful and beneficial flips are fractions of all agents whose final correctness differs from their initial correctness. Acceptance is the fraction of agent-rounds using a PBRC branch. First-correct time is zero for initially correct agents; we report its mean capped at round 8 and separately the fraction never correct by that horizon. A first correct prediction need not remain correct.

Two-sided 95% tt intervals use the 400 trial-level observations, with 399 degrees of freedom. Comparator intervals use paired within-trial differences. They are descriptive and not adjusted for multiple comparisons. Shared agents, methods, or noise settings are not treated as independent trials. The vectorized dynamics were checked against the reference router on prespecified trials 0 and 1, every regime/rate cell, all thresholds, agents, and rounds: 14,400 numerical transitions and acceptance decisions agreed exactly. Separate flooding checks also passed. These checks do not constitute a general correctness proof or a latency benchmark.

Results and limits.

Table 4 gives the ϵ=0.2\epsilon=0.2 slice; Figure 13 shows every error rate. Under independent errors, PBRC with k=3k=3 reaches 91.53% final accuracy, compared with 25.80% for no interaction and 81.69% for the specified social comparator. The paired accuracy difference from social pooling is 9.84 percentage points (95% CI 7.43–12.25); the Brier difference is −0.1092-0.1092 (95% CI [−0.1325,−0.0858][-0.1325,-0.0858]). However, PBRC with k=1k=1 or k=3k=3 has the same final accuracy as the matched evidence-only updater in every tested cell. When all five tokens arrive, their majority contains at least three tokens, so both thresholds apply the evidence-only operator by construction. This experiment therefore supplies no final-accuracy benefit of these gates over that updater; exact agreement in these samples does not establish population equivalence.

At independent error rate 0.2, k=3k=3 permits beneficial final flips for 67.76% of agents and harmful flips for 2.03%, with 78.18% of agent-rounds accepted. Raising the threshold to k=5k=5 lowers acceptance to 23.17% and final accuracy to 51.05%. Its capped mean first-correct time is 4.80 rounds, compared with 2.34 for k=3k=3 and 1.57 for evidence only; the corresponding never-correct fractions are 48.95%, 6.19%, and 4.68%. These jointly expose the cost of strict gating; the capped time alone is not an uncensored time-to-correction estimate.

Under fully correlated errors, k=1k=1 and k=3k=3 have identical final numerical beliefs in these trials, and k=5k=5 provides no substantive final-accuracy protection. Distinct issuer identities do not supply statistical independence. At error rate 0.5, the k=3k=3 Brier scores are 0.4385 (independent) and 0.4643 (correlated), worse than 0.3787 with no interaction despite higher classification accuracy. Thus neither admissibility nor improved top-label accuracy guarantees better probability forecasts. The controlled study demonstrates permitted correction and a safety–liveness trade-off within this model; practical LLM utility, semantic validation, acquisition bias, and verification latency remain outside this synthetic experiment. Section 13.10 separately examines answer-level admission with retrieved text and an imperfect NLI validator.

13.9 KAIROS: token-empty answer retention

We analyze 3,000 KAIROS [Song et al.(2025)] question instances under three conditions: independent RAW answers, SOCIAL interaction, and SOCIAL interaction with reflection. Conditions are paired by question and options, source dataset, and gold label. Outcomes use the recorded extracted predictions. A token-empty PBRC postprocessor applies conservative answer retention to the reflected outputs.

Table 5 retains every recorded row. The two-sided exact McNemar values against RAW are 1.476633709×10−71.476633709\times 10^{-7} for SOCIAL and 0.001315050.00131505 for SOCIAL with reflection. These are descriptive, unadjusted item-level comparisons. There are 2,999 unique dataset/question fingerprints: one BrainTeaser question occurs twice and is correct in every condition. Removing one copy leaves all discordant counts, and hence these exact-test values, unchanged. Shared benchmark sources and related items further limit an independent-item interpretation.

The token-empty postprocessor admits no evidence witness and returns RAW whenever a reflected answer differs. It therefore blocks all 697 reflected changes, including 327 harmful, 249 beneficial, and 121 neutral changes. Its accuracy is identically RAW accuracy; this is an answer-retention demonstration, not an independently generated reasoning improvement, an evidence-enabled result, or a numerical-belief compliance test.

The model is identified as gpt4o. An immutable model snapshot, complete decoding settings, all sampled completions, and full aggregation/extraction details are unavailable, limiting exact replication of model generation. RAW vote histograms contain eight votes in 2,945 instances and fewer in 55, with 103 modal ties. Analyses use the recorded decisions without imposing an additional tie-breaking rule.

13.10 SciFact: evidence-enabled claim verification

The SciFact [Wadden et al.(2020)] experiment evaluates answer admission using retrieved scientific passages and an imperfect NLI validator. It measures categorical answer-level behavior under unverified persuasive messages, complementing the token-empty KAIROS analysis. This instantiation does not implement the full numerical-belief model or KD45/PDL monitor.

Data, protocol, and models.

The primary main200 profile selects the first 200 of the 300 public development claims under the SHA-256 ordering of 20260730:claim_id. Selection uses no labels. Their gold classes are 82 SUPPORT, 41 CONTRADICT, and 77 NOT_ENOUGH_INFO (NEI). All 809 training claims are reserved for calibration and have disjoint IDs. Texts, labels, and evidence-document IDs come from the official SciFact archive identified in the protocol. These are development-set claim classifications; they are not official test-set or joint rationale-retrieval leaderboard scores.

The subject, treatment generator, and query generator use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [Qwen Team(2024)] through vLLM on the RunPod BF16 backend, at temperature zero and request seed zero. Maximum output lengths are 180, 260, and 64 tokens, respectively. The model revision is a09a35458c702b33eeacc393d103063234e8bc28. The NLI model is MoritzLaurer/DeBERTa-v3-base-mnli-fever-anli [Laurer(n.d.)], revision 6f5cf0a2b59cabb106aca4c287eed12e357e90eb, with a 384-token input limit. Hardware and library differences can prevent bit-identical fresh inference even with these settings.

The protocol fixes model revisions, configuration, selected IDs, and calibration before held-out generation; predictions are finalized before scoring. Generation reads unlabeled claims and the corpus, with a software guard blocking access to the score-only gold directory. Hashes record the local configuration; this procedure is not an independent public preregistration or a security boundary against administrator access. Held-out claims are excluded from tuning in this study; their absence from model pretraining is not established.

Acquisition and calibration.

BM25 searches all 5,183 corpus abstracts using the claim alone, with k1=1.5k_{1}=1.5 and b=0.75b=0.75. It retrieves eight documents and selects two sentences per document by lexical score, supplying up to 16 title-plus-sentence passages. A separate acquisition condition uses a model-generated query influenced by the majority messages. NLI treats each passage as premise and the claim as hypothesis. Let ss and cc be the maximum entailment and contradiction scores across retrieved passages. It abstains when max⁡(s,c)<θ\max(s,c)<\theta or |s−c|<m|s-c|<m; otherwise it selects SUPPORT if s>cs>c, and CONTRADICT otherwise. There were no equal-maxima ties in either held-out stream.

Training IDs are partitioned deterministically into 561 tuning and 248 internal-validation claims. The 45-point grid combines θ∈{0.50,0.55,…,0.90}\theta\in\{0.50,0.55,\ldots,0.90\} and m∈{0,0.05,…,0.20}m\in\{0,0.05,\ldots,0.20\}. The selection rule maximizes tuning macro-F1 among settings with non-abstaining precision at least 0.8; if none qualify, it maximizes macro-F1 over the whole grid, breaking ties by higher precision, coverage, and accuracy, then lower threshold and margin. No setting met the 0.8 target. The selected (θ,m)=(0.90,0)(\theta,m)=(0.90,0) has tuning precision 0.560 and internal-validation precision 0.508. These values are not semantic-truth guarantees. The selected setting remains fixed; the archived held-out grid is descriptive sensitivity analysis, not a replacement selection step.

Social interventions and comparators.

Each claim has eight subject outputs: RAW; terse, fluent, prestige, and three-message majority pressure; clean RAG; clean RAG plus majority pressure; and socially steered RAG plus majority pressure. One further call generates the treatment messages and one generates the acquisition query, yielding 2,000 recorded call outputs in total. The treatment stance opposes RAW’s SUPPORT/CONTRADICT label; when RAW is NEI, an ID-based rule chooses one of those labels. It never uses gold. The three majority messages come from one generator call, not three independent agents or independent evidence sources.

The generator is instructed to supply evidence-free rhetoric. Some outputs nevertheless assert unsupported studies, research, or data; for example, claim 845’s messages invoke studies without supplying a checkable source. We therefore interpret these conditions as unverified persuasive messages, including asserted empirical support, rather than a clean isolation of social prestige or stance from semantic persuasion. No externally validated evidence token is carried by these messages.

Citation-presence gating accepts a clean-RAG-majority answer if it cites any retrieved document, otherwise retaining RAW. Validator-only gating uses a non-abstaining clean NLI label, otherwise retaining RAW. Full PBRC considers the same clean-RAG-majority candidate and accepts only a non-abstaining token with a matching payload hash, exact claim/context binding, freshness, candidate-label agreement, and citation of the token’s document. Its fallback retains RAW. The steered-acquisition version uses the corresponding steered candidate and token. The nonconservative ablation uses the same clean admission gate but falls back to the social-majority answer. A token abstention is represented as NEI, so this gate cannot make an accepted correction to NEI; it can retain an initially correct NEI answer through fallback.

Results and acceptance errors.

Table 6 reports all methods. Full PBRC achieves 106/200=53.0%106/200=53.0\%, compared with 98/200=49.0%98/200=49.0\% for RAW, 123/200=61.5%123/200=61.5\% for clean RAG, and 67/200=33.5%67/200=33.5\% for clean RAG under majority pressure. Its paired difference from RAW is 4.0 percentage points, with a 5,000-resample paired-bootstrap percentile interval [−1.5,9.5][-1.5,9.5] points and exact p=0.215327p=0.215327. Thus the run does not establish an overall improvement over RAW and does not outperform clean RAG. Exploratory paired comparisons found 58 PBRC-only versus 19 pressured-RAG-only correct answers, but 22 PBRC-only versus 39 clean-RAG-only correct answers; these exploratory comparisons are secondary to the prespecified PBRC–RAW comparison.

Full PBRC accepts 51 non-fallback updates and uses fallback on 149 claims (74.5%). Only 36 accepted updates change the answer: 20 beneficial, 12 harmful, and four wrong-to-different-wrong changes. Across all 51 accepts, 31 are correct and 20 incorrect (accepted precision 60.8%); among the 36 actual changes, 20 are correct (55.6%). These denominators must not be conflated. Citation presence accepts 196 updates, of which 132 are incorrect; validator only accepts 108, of which 54 are incorrect. Steered PBRC accepts 48, of which 21 are incorrect, and scores 52.0%. The social-fallback ablation keeps the same 51 accepted updates but falls to 29.5% overall, illustrating the importance of fallback behavior in this setting.

The clean validator has 54.0% non-abstaining coverage and 50.0% precision among those labels. Retrieval finds at least one gold evidence document for 91.1% of the 123 evidence-bearing claims; this hit rate is not complete evidence-set or rationale recall. Steered retrieval changes all 200 query strings, has mean document-set Jaccard similarity 0.465 with clean retrieval, and reaches 91.9% hit rate. These acquisition results do not establish improved evidence quality: steered PBRC is slightly less accurate in this sample.

Parsing, checks, and scope.

All four subject parse errors and seven failed peer parses remain in the analysis; query parsing has no failures. Subject parse failure maps to NEI, which is also a scored class, rather than automatically counting as incorrect. A successful parse does not guarantee prompt compliance. For example, RAW supplies nonempty citations despite receiving no passages in 120/200 outputs. Clean RAG, clean RAG with majority, and steered RAG cite at least one document absent from their prompts on 13, six, and nine claims, respectively. The full gate requires the token’s document to be cited but does not reject every additional spurious citation. All scores use this same fixed parsing and admission policy.

The 108 non-abstaining clean tokens support controlled context, stale-token, and payload-mutation checks: full PBRC rejects every mutated case while the corresponding check-removal ablation accepts all; intact controls are accepted. These are secondary mechanism tests with constructed matching candidates, not naturally occurring attack rates. The token integrity field is an unkeyed SHA-256 content hash, not a digital signature: an attacker able to replace the token can recompute it. Freshness uses the fixed protocol clock 1700000000+11700000000+1 and a seven-day expiry interval, not observed wall-clock replay protection. The study therefore tests trusted in-process admission and syntactic consistency, not adversarial issuer authentication or semantic correctness.

The results quantify a conditional reduction in admitted social-pressure changes alongside retained errors and missed corrections. Generalization is limited by the use of one model, one selected development subset, one imperfect validator, and one fixed pressure protocol.

14 Limitations and open problems

The guarantees concern a fixed finite hypothesis space, explicit numerical beliefs, specified event semantics, and a faithful enforcement boundary. They do not show that an LLM internally represents these probabilities or reasons according to the contract. Hypothesis generation, changing ontologies, asynchronous delivery, expiry, revocation, and stateful spent-token tracking require additional formal treatment.

Evidence gating preserves the chosen fallback invariants on token-empty rounds. It does not guarantee truth, calibrated probabilities, useful learning, balanced evidence acquisition, or eventual correction. An overly restrictive contract can permanently retain an incorrect initial top hypothesis. Omission and query steering can bias evidence-bearing updates. An accepted witness establishes a contractual license; it is neither a complete numerical replay record nor proof of a unique causal explanation.

Token invariance is conditional on fixed context and annotations. General contracts may depend on message metadata, and sound-but-incomplete routers may make different acceptance decisions on token-equivalent events. Exact trajectory equivalence therefore needs the stated operator, fallback, and router assumptions. The normal-form construction needs suitable witnesses and first-order definability; it is not a representation theorem for arbitrary computational policies. Syntactic evidence gating is sufficient but not necessary for top preservation and confidence non-amplification.

Freshness limits the age of usable evidence but does not prevent repeated use inside a window. Authentication proves origin under a threat model, not semantic truth. Multi-attestation bounds require distinct authenticated identities and strong assumptions about honest validators and compromise dependence. Numerical claims must be enforced by a state-holding router or a correct operator-verification mechanism.

The logical results here establish soundness and exact monitoring of explicitly supplied finite models. All-model completeness and the finite-model property remain open questions for the combined system. Finite-prefix monitoring does not prove unobserved future behavior, and the belief modality needs semantics beyond a numerical log.

The simulations use idealized dynamics, with simulations I–V evaluated at one seed. The matched study uses fixed evidence weights, informative synthetic source claims, controlled label errors, and one pooling comparator. In KAIROS, token-empty gating preserves RAW by construction, while incomplete generation metadata limits exact replication. In SciFact, PBRC has no statistically established improvement over RAW and lower observed accuracy than clean RAG. The validator fails to meet the calibration precision target and admits incorrect answers; unsupported empirical assertions in peer messages preclude a pure-rhetoric interpretation. Claim dependence, one model/backend, a single selected development subset, and unadjusted comparisons limit generalization. Unkeyed token hashes and a synthetic protocol clock do not implement authenticated evidence or real-time replay security. Neither the simulation code nor the finite token-set reference router supplies a production semantic validator.

15 Conclusion

PBRC makes admissible belief changes a public contract: a selected evidence-bearing branch requires a checked witness and faithfully executed operator, while other steps use a declared fallback. Argmax-preserving, non-amplifying fallback yields precise token-empty invariants. A local transition characterization explains why those invariants do not require every safe protocol to use syntactic evidence gates.

Under the stated definability and witness assumptions, evidence splitting yields a behavior-preserving normal form; sound enforcement and token invariance support conditional trace equivalences. Flooding separates accumulated knowledge, governed by shortest-path distance, from incoming exposures, governed by positive-length walks. The logic supplies sound specifications and finite-log monitoring with an explicit operational bridge.

These results make admissibility and selected failure modes inspectable while leaving evidence truth, acquisition bias, numerical compliance, and practical utility as explicit obligations. The matched synthetic study shows beneficial revision but no final-accuracy gain over its evidence-only updater at the lower thresholds, and correlated errors defeat the benefit of distinct issuer identities. KAIROS experiments demonstrate the benefits and costs of retaining an initial answer. In SciFact, evidence-enabled PBRC attenuates the degradation associated with the specified majority-pressure condition, but admits wrong answers, has an inconclusive gain over RAW, and falls below clean RAG accuracy. This supports an auditable admission mechanism with explicit assumptions, not a general claim that stricter evidence gating improves reasoning.

Data and code availability. The accompanying source package contains the simulation implementations, finite token-set reference router, matched-study configurations and trajectories, KAIROS predictions, and SciFact protocol, calibration, retrieved passages, NLI scores, model outputs, admission decisions, and analysis scripts. The base simulation repository is https://github.com/alqithami/PBRC; its commit is specified in Section 13.1. Stored-output analyses can be reproduced without model inference. Third-party data and model licenses apply to the corresponding artifacts.

Appendix A Soundness and finite-model monitoring for CDDL

A.1 Proof of soundness

Fix any model in the class of Theorem 23. Propositional tautologies are valid by Boolean semantics. Normality for either modality follows because a universal successor quantifier preserves implication. Modus ponens preserves truth at each state. Necessitation preserves global validity, since a globally valid formula holds at every accessible successor.

For BiB_{i}, seriality proves 𝐃\mathbf{D}: Bi​φB_{i}\varphi and Bi​¬φB_{i}\neg\varphi cannot both hold since an accessible successor exists. Transitivity proves 𝟒\mathbf{4}: if all successors of ww satisfy φ\varphi, every successor of a successor is also a successor of ww, so Bi​Bi​φB_{i}B_{i}\varphi holds. Euclideanness proves 𝟓\mathbf{5}: if ¬Bi​φ\neg B_{i}\varphi holds at ww, choose vv with w​Ri​vwR_{i}v and ¬φ\neg\varphi at vv. For every uu with w​Ri​uwR_{i}u, Euclideanness gives u​Ri​vuR_{i}v, hence ¬Bi​φ\neg B_{i}\varphi at uu. Thus Bi​¬Bi​φB_{i}\neg B_{i}\varphi holds at ww.

The sequence axiom follows because an α;β\alpha;\beta successor is precisely a β\beta successor of an α\alpha successor. Choice is union, so universal quantification over it is the conjunction of the two boxes. A test has only the identity edge at states satisfying its formula, proving [ψ​?]​φ↔(ψ→φ)[\psi?]\varphi\leftrightarrow(\psi\to\varphi).

For 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐫\mathbf{Star}, if [α∗]​φ[\alpha^{\ast}]\varphi holds at ww, the zero-length path gives φ\varphi at ww. Prefixing an arbitrary finite path by an α\alpha step shows [α]​[α∗]​φ[\alpha][\alpha^{\ast}]\varphi. Conversely, assume φ∧[α]​[α∗]​φ\varphi\land[\alpha][\alpha^{\ast}]\varphi at ww. Any finite α\alpha path from ww either has length zero or consists of a first step followed by an α∗\alpha^{\ast} path. The respective conjunct ensures φ\varphi at its endpoint. This proves the star equivalence.

For 𝐈𝐧𝐝\mathbf{Ind}, suppose φ→[α]​φ\varphi\to[\alpha]\varphi is globally valid. Starting at any state satisfying φ\varphi, induction on finite path length shows that each α\alpha-reachable state satisfies φ\varphi. Therefore φ→[α∗]​φ\varphi\to[\alpha^{\ast}]\varphi is globally valid. Applying these axiom and rule facts inductively to any finite derivation proves Theorem 23.

A.2 Finite-model algorithm and correctness

Let WW be the supplied finite state set. Represent a formula by its truth set and a program by a binary relation on WW. Atoms use the supplied valuation; negation uses complement in WW; conjunction uses intersection. For Bi​φB_{i}\varphi, retain exactly states whose RiR_{i} successors all belong to the already computed truth set of φ\varphi. For [α]​φ[\alpha]\varphi, use the same universal-successor operation with the computed RαR_{\alpha}.

For programs, atomic actions use supplied relations, choice uses union, sequence uses Boolean relational composition, and ψ​?\psi? uses the identity restricted to the computed truth set of ψ\psi. For α∗\alpha^{\ast}, start with the identity and repeatedly add pairs reachable by one further RαR_{\alpha} step until no pair changes. There are only |W|2|W|^{2} pairs, so the procedure terminates. Its invariant is that after rr extensions it contains exactly the pairs connected by paths of length at most rr; stabilization therefore equals reflexive transitive closure.

Mutual induction on the finite syntax trees of formulas and programs now proves each computed set and relation equals its semantic interpretation. Tests contain strictly smaller formula subtrees, and modalities contain strictly smaller program and formula subtrees, so the recursion is well founded. Using Boolean matrices and a Floyd–Warshall transitive-closure computation, an implementation takes at most O⁡(L​|W|3)O(L|W|^{3}) time and O⁡(L​|W|2)O(L|W|^{2}) storage, where LL is total formula/program syntax size; this deliberately coarse bound includes closure and composition. Event parsing, token validation, and first-order trigger evaluation are separate preprocessing costs. This proves Theorem 24.

For a finite run, Lemma 6 supplies the action relation. Enumerating reachable source indices then checking their actual successors returns the earliest violation of either displayed PBRC invariant. No doxastic accessibility relation is inferred from numerical beliefs.
